full_text: US$60 Million Zambia Solar Investment Targets Energy Security Zambia solar investment of $60m with ARC Power and Kiyona Energy signals rising demand for bankable renewables in Southern Africa. The post US$60 Million Zambia Solar Investment Targets Energy Security appeared first on FurtherAfrica. A new Zambia solar investment of US$60 million, agreed between ARC Power and Kiyona Energy, marks a pivotal step in the country’s drive to cut hydropower dependence and build a more climate-resilient power system.   The deal gives fresh momentum to Zambia’s push for energy diversification. For investors, it signals rising demand for bankable renewable projects under innovative private-led financing structures that limit upfront fiscal strain. Financing model aims to ease pressure on the state ARC Power and Kiyona Energy signed a FUSE agreement in June 2026 targeting an initial investment of up to US$60 million to accelerate solar generation in Zambia, as part of a broader programme to deploy new solar infrastructure in the country. The partnership targets new solar infrastructure across the country to support energy security, expand access and reduce exposure to hydrological risk. Hydropower still provides around 85–90% of Zambia’s electricity, leaving the system highly vulnerable to drought-driven output swings. Recent dry spells have forced Zambia to ration power and cut exports, highlighting the need for diversification. Policymakers have since moved solar up the agenda, backed by regulatory reforms and a clearer project pipeline. ARC Power plans to use its FUSE (Future Utility Solutions for Electrification) investment model to structure the investment. Under its FUSE model, ARC Power designs, finances, builds and operates energy assets under long-term contractual arrangements with offtakers, providing predictable cash flows for investors while reducing upfront public spending. This approach lowers the requirement for immediate public spending and shifts early project risk to the private sector, while securing predictable cash flows for investors over time. The structure aligns with wider efforts by lenders such as the World Bank and the African Development Bank to crowd in private capital through programme-based electrification and risk-sharing tools. For Zambia, it offers a way to accelerate grid-strengthening and generation capacity without overloading the sovereign balance sheet. Drought risk turns solar into a strategic asset The deal lands as prolonged droughts across Southern Africa strain hydropower reservoirs, including Zambia’s Kariba dam. Lower water levels have cut available capacity and exposed the cost of reliance on a single dominant technology. Solar, by contrast, benefits from the country’s high irradiation and short construction timelines, making it attractive both as baseload support and as a hedge against climate volatility. The ARC Power and Kiyona transaction adds to a growing pipeline of utility-scale projects in Zambia’s solar sector. Recent utility-scale solar schemes in Zambia include projects such as the 54 MW Bangweulu and 34 MW Ngonye plants under the Scaling Solar program, along with additional IPP-led projects under development backed by development financiers and commercial lenders. Kiyona Energy has been involved in developing renewable energy projects in Zambia, underscoring its local credentials. These projects support Zambia’s wider push to expand access, reduce load-shedding and underpin industrial growth. As more miners, agro-processing companies and manufacturers seek reliable power, demand for independent producers and corporate offtake structures is set to rise. In that context, the ARC Power model could provide a template for bundling smaller grid and generation assets into bankable portfolios. For investors, this Zambia solar investment with ARC Power and Kiyona Energy highlights three key signals. First, energy diversification is now central to Zambia’s macro and industrial strategy, which supports continuity of policy for renewables. Second, deal structures that blend private capital with eventual public ownership are gaining traction, potentially creating repeatable platforms rather than one-off projects. Third, drought risk is no longer a tail event but a planning assumption, which strengthens the case for climate-resilient infrastructure across the region. Further phases under the partnership are already anticipated. The performance of this first tranche — on execution, grid integration and tariff stability — will be closely watched. Investors should track how quickly capacity is added, how FUSE contracts are priced and whether similar models emerge in neighbouring markets, as these will shape the next wave of scalable utility-scale renewables in Southern Africa. The post New Expansion Positions Angola as Emerging Aluminium Producer appeared first on FurtherAfrica. The Angola aluminium project has reached a new milestone, with China’s SINOMACH securing a US$245 million Phase II EPC contract for the Huatong Aluminium Industrial Park at the Barra do Dande Free Trade Zone in Bengo Province.   SINOMACH agreement advances one of Angola’s most ambitious industrial diversification projects and strengthens efforts to build value-added manufacturing capacity beyond the oil sector. Aluminium project enters next growth phase The Phase II contract was signed on 11 June during the 17th International Infrastructure Investment and Construction Forum and Exhibition. The contract was awarded to SINOMACH International Engineering (Jiangsu) Co., Ltd. and will add 120,000 tonnes of annual electrolytic aluminium production capacity. This follows the inauguration of the project’s first 120,000-tonne production line in January 2026 by President João Lourenço. The Huatong Aluminium Industrial Park is being developed in five phases over an estimated eight to ten years. Total investment is expected to reach approximately US$1.6 billion. Phase I alone required around US$250 million in capital expenditure and is expected to generate roughly 1,200 direct jobs. For investors, the choice of an engineering, procurement and construction (EPC) model is significant. EPC contracts place responsibility for design, procurement, construction and commissioning under a single contractor, helping improve project coordination and delivery discipline. However, execution performance remains a critical factor given the scale and complexity of the development. Hydropower underpins the investment case The long-term viability of the project depends heavily on access to reliable and affordable electricity. Primary aluminium production is among the most energy-intensive industrial processes in the world. The Hall-Héroult smelting process typically requires between 13,000 and 15,000 kilowatt-hours of electricity for every tonne of aluminium produced. As a result, energy costs are often the single most important determinant of competitiveness. Angola is seeking to leverage its growing hydropower capacity to support energy-intensive industries. The country’s electricity system already benefits from the Laúca Dam, while the large-scale Caculo Cabaça Hydroelectric Project remains under development. Together, these projects strengthen the case for establishing domestic aluminium production and other power-intensive industries. The aluminium park also aligns with Angola’s broader industrialisation agenda. The Barra do Dande Free Trade Zone was created to attract manufacturing investment, support exports and deepen economic diversification away from hydrocarbons. Strategic significance for Angola and Africa The project has implications beyond Angola. Primary aluminium production remains concentrated in a limited number of facilities across Africa. Additional capacity in Angola would expand the continent’s industrial processing base and create opportunities across logistics, construction, engineering services and downstream manufacturing. The timing also aligns with growing global demand for supply-chain diversification and energy-transition materials. Aluminium plays a critical role in renewable energy systems, electric vehicles, transmission infrastructure and advanced manufacturing. For investors, the central question remains execution. The project’s success will depend on construction timelines, power availability and the smooth commissioning of future phases. If delivered as planned, the Huatong Aluminium Industrial Park could become one of Angola’s most important industrial assets and a flagship example of how hydropower resources and industrial policy can be combined to support long-term economic diversification. South Africa, or SA as locals call it, is a completely unique experience. Whether you’re an avid traveler seeking something new or a newcomer choosing your first destination, SA will captivate you with its natural beauty, delicious cuisine, and friendly locals. This country takes pride in its cultural unity. Yet, you will rarely find a place with so much versatility. Before coming there, however, you should know a few important things. 1. Have Cash on You Many big cafes and restaurants in South Africa accept debit and credit cards, but you should always have some cash on you. Smaller stores, roadside merchants, and some taxi drivers have not adopted digital payments and will not do so in the near future. Moreover, cash is necessary for tipping — an essential cultural practice. Since base salaries are incredibly low, especially for service workers such as servers and gas attendants, tips are paramount to them. It’s common to leave a bigger tip, around 20%, for good service. Depending on additional assistance, you may leave more, and it will always be appreciated by whoever served you that time. 2. Watch Out For Power Outages SA’s primary energy supplier, Eskom, introduced load-shedding back in 2007. Since then, the country has been living with blackouts. It’s a common experience, and although many locals are used to it, no one likes it. Nowadays, the energy supply is more stable, but the power crisis is still ongoing. So, everyone travelling to SA should be aware of the situation. Electricity outages are unplanned in most cases and might last from several hours to a couple of days. During that time, you won’t be able to charge your devices, turn on the lights, and so on. It is advised to bring a good power bank when traveling, just in case. You can use the EskomSePush app to check when the area you are staying in may be affected by the outages. When there’s no Wi-Fi connectivity, you can still use mobile data and set a hotspot for your devices. To minimize roaming charges, however, opt for an eSIM app. It’ll connect to the local cell towers and provide you with a generally stable connection. 3. Be Mindful of Your Surroundings Power outages might be a culture shock, but it’s not the worst thing you can encounter in South Africa. Violent crimes, strikes, and similar incidents can startle the tourists. Robbery, assault, mugging, and carjacking mostly occur in the downtown areas after dark. Kidnappers often target U.S. citizens to kidnap them for ransom or force them to withdraw money. As for protests and strikes, they start very suddenly and occur often. Unfortunately, they turn violent all the time and can interrupt many public services. So, you should always be aware of your surroundings when you’re out in the city. Do not travel alone, and do not leave the hotel after dark. Don’t join big crowds. Hide your costly accessories and jewelry when walking around and avoid withdrawing a lot of cash publicly. 4. Rent a Car While South Africa is gorgeous, public transportation there is not the best. There are long-distance bus and train routes, but they often miss smaller destinations and can be pretty expensive. Furthermore, most of them are unreliable — not recommended for tourists who don’t know the country. Renting a car is the best option, for sure. Fortunately, all the bigger car rental companies are just as good in SA, and there are many road trip routes to choose from. Book ahead and be aware of common unspoken driving rules to make the best out of your experience. For example, since many roads are single-lane, drivers often use the emergency lane with a yellow line as a backup. Also, stay cautious when on the road: keep your windows up when possible, leave a gap in the front when stopping at the traffic lights, and lock the doors to avoid incidents. 5. Stay Connected Through Public Wi-Fi When there are no power outages, you can easily find free Wi-Fi in bigger cities. Restaurants, coffee shops, and hotels will accommodate you so you can stay connected with your loved ones. Use Wi-Fi finder apps to locate the nearby networks, whether at the airport or at the mall. Remember that South Africa is not exempt from bad actors online, and you should always secure your connection when connecting to a network. A VPN comparison can help you find the best tool for your needs, as a VPN encrypts your traffic, making it impossible for unauthorized users to access it. 6. Pack Appropriate Clothing To some, South Africa looks like a hot region. But it’s not always like that. Its waters can be cold, mountains snowy, and beaches stormy. So, tourists packing a T-shirt and shorts can definitely freeze their fingers off if they’re not careful. SA’s summers are extremely hot. From December to February, you will face heatwaves and occasional rain showers. Depending on the region, the weather might be humid or completely dry, so always check the weather beforehand. Pack light, breathable fabrics. Also, pack a big sun hat to protect your head and face. In March and April, however, the weather becomes more bearable. It’s not too hot or cold, and you can finally wear something with more coverage. Autumn to early winter in May and June stands around 15℃, and many South Africans complain about the cold. At this point, Cape Town is experiencing wet and windy conditions. In September and October (the SA’s spring), the country is still a little cold, but November and December are coming closer with beach parties and early Christmas festivities. Ready for Your South Africa Trip South Africa is an incredibly versatile country with friendly people and viral positive energy. Although you should be aware of common crimes, as long as you stay aware of your surroundings and stick to simple safety rules, you will be okay. Additionally, don’t forget to carry some cash with you — especially important for the tipping culture. Know when the power will be off, pack clothing appropriate to the season, and rent a car to explore SA efficiently.   The post Packing for South Africa? 6 Things You Need to Know appeared first on FurtherAfrica.

Keypoints: Lower house passes bill with two-thirds majority Constitutional changes could extend Mnangagwa’s rule to 2030 Senate approval expected as political battle intensifies ZIBABWE’S lower house of parliament has approved constitutional changes that would extend President Emmerson Mnangagwa’s tenure to 2030, moving one of the country’s most controversial political reforms a step closer to becoming law. The proposed constitutional changes have become one of Zimbabwe’s most contentious political issues, with supporters arguing they will improve stability and governance while opponents warning they could weaken democratic safeguards and extend the rule of the incumbent president. Lawmakers approved the bill with 216 votes on Thursday, comfortably exceeding the two-thirds majority required for constitutional amendments. The bill now heads to the Senate, where the ruling ZANU-PF party and its allies are also expected to command enough support for passage. Constitutional battle intensifies The vote marks a significant step in a plan that has been gathering momentum within ZANU-PF for more than a year. If enacted, the reforms would extend presidential terms from five years to seven years and defer elections currently scheduled for 2028 until 2030. Supporters argue the changes would promote political stability and allow governments more time to implement long-term development programmes. Critics see them as an attempt to prolong Mnangagwa’s stay in power. The 83-year-old leader is constitutionally required to leave office at the end of his current term in 2028. However, the proposed amendments would effectively add two years to his presidency, allowing him to remain in office until 2030. According to government proposals previously reported and verified by Africa Briefing in Zimbabwe bill seeks to extend Mnangagwa rule to 2030, the reforms would also replace direct presidential elections with a parliamentary vote, a move opponents argue would significantly reduce public participation in selecting the country’s leader. The proposed reforms have been championed by Mnangagwa’s supporters, who began publicly calling for an extension of his leadership several years ago. Africa Briefing previously reported in ZANU-PF plans Mnangagwa term extension to 2030 that party leaders argued additional time was needed to preserve continuity and stability in government programmes. Opposition and legal challenges Opposition politicians, civil society groups and some veterans of Zimbabwe’s liberation struggle have accused the government of undermining constitutional safeguards designed to prevent the concentration of power. The dispute has also exposed widening divisions within the ruling party. Earlier Africa Briefing reporting in Zanu-PF erupts over Mnangagwa’s 2030 bid documented growing tensions among rival factions over succession planning and the future direction of the party. The involvement of liberation war veterans is particularly significant because many have historically been associated with the ruling establishment. Their opposition has highlighted growing unease among some traditional supporters of ZANU-PF over the proposed constitutional changes. Legal challenges brought by activists and veterans have so far failed to halt the process after courts dismissed recent applications on procedural grounds. Nevertheless, critics are expected to continue exploring legal and political avenues to resist the reforms as they move through the legislative process. Government supporters reject accusations of democratic backsliding. They argue that longer terms would reduce the frequency and cost of elections while providing continuity for economic reforms and national development strategies. Regional trend under scrutiny The debate has also drawn attention because it mirrors constitutional changes seen elsewhere on the continent. Countries including Cameroon and Uganda have faced criticism after constitutional or legal amendments enabled long-serving leaders to remain in office beyond previously expected timelines. The debate also reflects a wider continental trend. Africa Briefing recently examined similar constitutional disputes in DR Congo reform push tests term limits, where proposed reforms have likewise sparked debate over presidential tenure, constitutional safeguards and democratic accountability. Analysts say constitutional amendments affecting presidential tenure have become a recurring source of political tension across several African states, often triggering debates over democratic accountability, institutional checks and balances, and the peaceful transfer of power. For supporters, such reforms can provide continuity and policy stability. For critics, they risk weakening constitutional guardrails designed to prevent the excessive concentration of executive authority. Senate vote expected The Senate is expected to consider the legislation in the coming weeks. Given ZANU-PF’s dominance in both chambers, observers believe approval is likely unless fresh legal obstacles emerge. The ruling party’s influence in the upper chamber means the legislation is widely expected to pass unless opposition groups secure a legal intervention before the vote. If approved and signed into law, the constitutional changes would represent one of the most significant restructurings of Zimbabwe’s political system since the adoption of the 2013 constitution. Keypoints: Kenya seeks to convert diplomatic visibility into economic gains Debt, climate finance and investment remain Nairobi’s priorities Domestic governance will determine whether foreign policy delivers results PRESIDENT William Ruto’s presence at the G7 summit in France should be viewed as more than a diplomatic courtesy. It forms part of Kenya’s broader effort to convert international visibility into economic leverage at a time when the country faces mounting debt pressures, fiscal constraints and growing public discontent. The symbolism is significant. Kenya is no longer content to be a passive observer in global economic conversations. Nairobi increasingly seeks to position itself as a leading African voice on debt reform, climate finance, fairer risk pricing and the restructuring of the international financial system. That ambition is not misplaced. The global financial architecture continues to disadvantage many African economies. Countries across the continent often face higher borrowing costs, elevated risk premiums and assessments based on models that frequently overstate instability while undervaluing opportunity. Kenya’s case for financial reform This is the argument Ruto has consistently carried from Nairobi to major international forums. At the Africa Forward Summit in Nairobi, African leaders called for a reassessment of how risk is priced, how private capital can be mobilised and how African countries can gain access to cheaper, longer-term development finance. The G7 summit provides Kenya with a larger platform from which to advance that agenda. The question, however, is whether greater visibility will translate into meaningful outcomes. The challenge is that the G7 remains a club of the world’s most advanced economies. Its communiqués and commitments matter, but they often move more slowly than the crises confronting developing nations. Recent discussions around sovereign debt vulnerabilities suggest growing recognition that developing countries need better tools to avoid financial distress. Yet recognition alone does not provide relief. African economies require lower borrowing costs, fairer refinancing arrangements, credible guarantees, accessible climate finance and development support that remains consistent even when political priorities shift in wealthier countries. The domestic political challenge These international debates have direct implications for Kenya’s domestic politics. Debt servicing continues to absorb significant public resources, while fiscal consolidation measures have increased pressure on households and businesses. The memory of the Finance Bill protests remains fresh. Many young Kenyans have demonstrated that they are unwilling to accept policies they perceive as punitive, particularly when concerns about corruption, waste and accountability persist. As the 2027 elections draw closer, Ruto faces a difficult balancing act. He must reassure lenders and investors while avoiding policies that further alienate voters. This is why the G7 matters beyond foreign policy. If Kenya’s international engagement fails to expand fiscal space at home, it risks being dismissed as political theatre. If, however, it helps attract investment, reduce borrowing costs, unlock climate finance and ease pressure for additional taxation, then it becomes an exercise in effective statecraft. The distinction lies in delivery. Visibility versus leverage Ruto’s foreign policy has long reflected this tension. Early in his administration, critics viewed aspects of Kenya’s diplomacy as reactive or inconsistent, citing issues such as the Sahrawi policy reversal, the controversy surrounding the Haiti deployment and the optics of frequent foreign travel during a period of economic hardship. Over time, however, the strategy has become more recognisable as an effort to diversify Kenya’s international partnerships. The United States, Europe, China, Gulf states and multilateral institutions all remain important to Nairobi. In an increasingly multipolar world, Kenya cannot afford diplomatic narrowness. Yet diversification must be accompanied by strategic discipline. A country can engage multiple partners and still gain little leverage if it lacks clear objectives. The G7 summit should therefore be more than another entry in Kenya’s growing catalogue of international appearances. It should serve as an opportunity to advance a focused agenda centred on debt restructuring, fairer credit ratings, climate investment, technology transfer, market access and support for youth entrepreneurship. Governance remains the decisive factor This is where domestic governance becomes critical. Kenya cannot credibly advocate for reform abroad while undermining confidence at home. If Nairobi seeks to lead conversations on financial reform, it must also demonstrate commitment to prudent public spending, anti-corruption measures, transparent procurement and institutional accountability. The proposed international anti-corruption centre in Nairobi may strengthen Kenya’s diplomatic profile, but citizens will judge its success by tangible outcomes rather than ceremonial launches. Foreign policy is often described as an extension of domestic policy. In Kenya’s case, that principle now operates in both directions. International platforms can strengthen the country’s position, but domestic frustrations can equally weaken its credibility. Ruto may persuasively highlight the inequities of the global financial system, yet many Kenyans will continue to ask why governance shortcomings at home remain unresolved. International recognition cannot substitute for domestic trust. The real test of Kenya’s G7 moment Ultimately, the significance of Kenya’s participation in the G7 summit will not be measured by photographs, diplomatic statements or warm receptions. Kenya has already demonstrated its ability to attract international attention. The more important question is whether that visibility can be transformed into bargaining power that delivers tangible benefits to citizens. At the G7, Ruto is effectively speaking to two audiences. The first is global: lenders, investors, governments and institutions that want Kenya to appear fiscally disciplined and strategically valuable. The second is domestic: citizens seeking jobs, lower living costs, tax relief and greater government accountability. The success of the visit will therefore be measured not by optics but by outcomes. Global visibility is valuable. Leverage is more valuable still. And in an election season, delivery remains the only form of diplomacy that voters truly recognise. Mikhail Nyamweya is a political and foreign affairs analyst and holds an MSc in African Studies from the University of OxfordThe post Op-Ed: Can Ruto turn G7 visibility into leverage? first appeared on Africa Briefing.

Keypoints: UK jury acquits Diezani Alison-Madueke after a decade-long corruption investigation Verdict highlights the difficulty of prosecuting complex cross-border corruption cases Outcome raises questions about Britain’s anti-corruption strategy and accountability efforts BRITAIN’S decade-long effort to prosecute former Nigerian oil minister Diezani Alison-Madueke ended in acquittal this week, raising fresh questions about whether Western anti-corruption agencies can successfully prove complex international corruption cases in court. The verdict matters beyond Alison-Madueke herself. It highlights the growing challenge facing anti-corruption agencies worldwide: transforming years of investigations, international cooperation and public suspicion into criminal convictions that can survive judicial scrutiny. After more than a decade of investigations, legal battles and international scrutiny, a jury at London’s Southwark Crown Court found Alison-Madueke not guilty on six bribery-related charges. The verdict brought to a close a case that British authorities had long viewed as a test of their ability to pursue alleged corruption involving senior foreign officials and international financial networks, according to Reuters. A verdict with implications beyond Nigeria The ruling extends far beyond the fate of one former minister. For years, the UK has sought to position itself as a global leader in combating illicit finance, money laundering and foreign corruption. London has tightened anti-money laundering rules, increased scrutiny of politically exposed persons and expanded international cooperation aimed at tracing suspect financial flows. Against that backdrop, the Alison-Madueke case became a flagship prosecution. Questions around accountability have long shaped Nigeria’s energy sector. Previous reform efforts, including measures aimed at improving transparency and recovering lost revenues, have formed part of a broader push to strengthen oversight in Africa’s largest oil-producing economy. Nigeria’s energy-sector reform programme sought to recover billions of dollars in unpaid revenues while increasing transparency across the industry. British authorities became involved after Alison-Madueke settled in Britain following her departure from office. Investigators believed some of the financial arrangements and benefits under scrutiny were linked to UK-based assets and transactions. British investigators first began examining allegations involving the former minister more than a decade ago. Prosecutors argued that she enjoyed a lavish lifestyle funded by influential figures in Nigeria’s oil and gas sector who hoped to benefit from government contracts. Alison-Madueke consistently denied wrongdoing and maintained she never accepted bribes. The jury ultimately sided with the defence. The evidence challenge The outcome has renewed debate about a persistent problem facing anti-corruption agencies worldwide: proving elite corruption in court is often far more difficult than identifying suspicious conduct. The challenge extends beyond Nigeria. According to regional assessments, corruption and illicit financial flows continue to impose significant economic costs across Africa, reinforcing calls for stronger institutions and more effective enforcement mechanisms. As Africa Briefing previously reported, Africa loses $88bn annually to graft. Unlike conventional criminal cases, major corruption investigations frequently involve offshore entities, multiple jurisdictions, intermediaries, luxury benefits and financial transactions spanning several countries. Investigators may spend years assembling evidence only to encounter the demanding burden of proof required in criminal proceedings. The challenge was highlighted by anti-corruption campaigners following the verdict. ‘This case has exposed just how tough it is to investigate and prosecute alleged corruption involving political elites,’ Zainab Saleem of Spotlight on Corruption told Reuters. Her assessment captures the dilemma facing enforcement agencies. Public concern about corruption can be substantial, yet translating allegations into criminal convictions requires evidence capable of persuading a jury beyond reasonable doubt. Was this a corruption case or an ethics case? One of the most significant aspects of the trial received less public attention than the allegations themselves. Reuters reported that British prosecutors did not argue Alison-Madueke awarded contracts to companies that were not entitled to receive them. Instead, they sought to establish that it was improper for her to accept benefits from individuals and businesses involved in sectors under her authority. That distinction may prove critical in understanding the verdict. Cases involving direct evidence of manipulated procurement processes can be easier for juries to understand. Cases centred on influence, relationships and benefits are often more difficult because prosecutors must demonstrate not only that advantages were received, but that those advantages amounted to criminal bribery. The result underscores how legal standards can diverge from public expectations. Nigeria questions remain The acquittal is also likely to reignite debate in Nigeria about accountability and governance within the country’s oil sector. That debate remains active. Nigerian anti-corruption agencies continue to argue that reforms and enforcement measures are producing results, even as concerns persist about transparency, public trust and institutional effectiveness. Earlier this year Nigeria’s anti-graft agency, the EFCC, defended Nigeria’s anti-corruption record while acknowledging the scale of the challenge. Alison-Madueke served as petroleum minister during a period when concerns about transparency, oil revenue management and institutional oversight frequently dominated public discourse. While the UK verdict settles the criminal case before the British courts, it does not resolve wider questions about governance reforms, transparency standards and accountability mechanisms that have shaped discussions around Nigeria’s energy sector for more than a decade. For many Nigerians, the broader debate has always extended beyond one individual to the effectiveness of institutions tasked with safeguarding public resources. Personal vindication, institutional questions Following the verdict, Alison-Madueke described the outcome as the end of a prolonged ordeal. ‘For 11 long, gruelling years this case has hung over my head and has tormented me and my family,’ she said in a statement released through her spokesperson. She added that years of scrutiny and allegations had finally come to an end. British authorities adopted a more restrained response. ‘We respect the decision of the jury,’ a spokesperson for Britain’s National Crime Agency told Reuters. Yet behind that statement lies a difficult reality. The acquittal represents a major setback for investigators who invested years pursuing one of Britain’s most prominent foreign corruption cases. Lessons for future anti-corruption efforts The verdict arrives as Western governments intensify efforts to combat illicit financial flows from developing economies and strengthen enforcement against politically exposed individuals. Yet the outcome demonstrates how difficult it remains to convert cross-border investigations into criminal convictions, even when authorities devote substantial resources and years of effort to a case. Many governance specialists increasingly argue that stronger procurement systems, beneficial ownership transparency, asset recovery mechanisms and financial oversight may produce more durable results than lengthy courtroom battles. Those arguments align with wider discussions about governance reform in Nigeria, where policymakers are attempting to improve transparency, accountability and efficiency across key sectors of the economy. Recent analysis by Africa Briefing highlighted how ongoing economic and energy-sector reforms are increasingly being judged on their ability to strengthen institutions as well as deliver growth. The Alison-Madueke case illustrates the limits of prosecution as a standalone anti-corruption tool. For Britain, the verdict raises uncomfortable questions about whether existing legal frameworks are sufficient to tackle sophisticated international corruption cases. For African governments pursuing accountability reforms, it offers a reminder that allegations and investigations alone are not enough. Convictions require evidence that can withstand the highest level of judicial scrutiny. Even where prosecutions fail, lengthy investigations can carry lasting political and reputational consequences for the individuals and institutions involved. More than a decade after the investigation began, the case has become a reminder that in the fight against elite corruption, suspicion may be relatively easy to establish, but proof remains extraordinarily difficult to deliver.The post UK loses landmark Nigeria corruption case first appeared on Africa Briefing.

Keypoints: Study links mining expansion to major forest loss Infrastructure causes most deforestation impacts Energy transition creates new environmental dilemma AFRICA’S position at the centre of the global energy transition is becoming increasingly valuable. The continent holds vast reserves of copper, cobalt, lithium, manganese, graphite and other minerals essential for electric vehicles, renewable energy systems and battery storage technologies. As governments and corporations race to secure supplies of these critical minerals, Africa is attracting unprecedented investment. Yet new research suggests the environmental costs of this mining boom may be far greater than previously understood. The findings arrive as African governments seek to capitalise on surging demand for critical minerals needed for the global energy transition. While mining promises jobs, revenues and industrial growth, the study suggests the environmental costs may be significantly larger than previously understood, creating a new policy dilemma for resource-rich states. According to research published in Nature by scientists from the University of Sheffield, mining-related activities contributed to the loss of approximately 187,000 hectares of forest across sub-Saharan Africa between 2001 and 2020. More strikingly, the researchers concluded that for every hectare of forest directly cleared for mining, another 34 hectares were lost through associated activities such as road construction, settlements, transport corridors and agricultural expansion around mining projects. Why the findings matter For decades, environmental assessments have focused primarily on the land directly occupied by mines. The new research suggests this approach captures only a fraction of mining’s true impact. According to the study, most forest loss occurs outside mining concessions. New roads open previously inaccessible areas to farming and logging. Workers migrate into mining regions, creating demand for housing and services. Infrastructure networks expand to support production and exports. The result is a much larger transformation of landscapes than official mine footprints would suggest. This finding is particularly significant because many of Africa’s mineral-rich regions overlap with some of the continent’s most ecologically important forests. These forests store carbon, regulate rainfall patterns, support biodiversity and sustain millions of people through agriculture, forestry and ecosystem services. The study’s authors argue that policymakers and investors may need to rethink how mining impacts are assessed, monitored and mitigated if environmental commitments are to remain credible. The energy transition paradox The findings expose a growing contradiction at the heart of global climate policy. The world is seeking to reduce carbon emissions through electric vehicles, renewable energy systems and clean technologies. Achieving these goals requires vast quantities of minerals, many of which are found in Africa. Copper is essential for electricity transmission and renewable energy systems. Cobalt remains critical to many battery technologies. Lithium underpins electric vehicle production. Demand for these resources is expected to grow substantially over the coming decades. Yet extracting these materials is placing increasing pressure on forest ecosystems that also play a vital role in combating climate change. In effect, the world risks protecting the climate through one mechanism while weakening another. For African countries, this creates a delicate balancing act. They are being encouraged to supply the minerals needed for global decarbonisation while also preserving ecosystems that contribute to climate resilience and biodiversity protection. Ghana, Congo and Zambia under pressure The implications are already visible across several African mining jurisdictions. In Ghana, concerns over mining-related deforestation and water pollution have intensified political debates surrounding forest reserves and environmental protection. Illegal mining, known locally as galamsey, has become a major national issue, while industrial mining projects continue to expand in several regions. The Democratic Republic of Congo, which supplies a significant share of the world’s cobalt, faces growing scrutiny over the environmental consequences of expanding mineral production. As demand for battery minerals rises, pressure on surrounding ecosystems is expected to increase. Zambia’s plans to increase copper production are similarly raising questions about how economic ambitions can be balanced with environmental management. Meanwhile, Guinea’s expanding bauxite industry highlights the broader challenge facing mineral-rich African states. Guinea is home to some of the world’s largest bauxite reserves and has become a strategic supplier to the global aluminium industry, making environmental governance an increasingly important consideration as production expands. The new scramble for minerals The study arrives amid intensifying geopolitical competition for African resources. China remains deeply embedded across Africa’s mining sector through investments, infrastructure projects and processing facilities. Western governments, concerned about supply chain security, are increasingly pursuing alternative sources of critical minerals. The United States and European Union have both expanded efforts to secure access to strategic minerals, while Gulf investors are also increasing their presence across the continent. This competition creates opportunities for African countries to negotiate better terms, attract investment and promote local processing industries. However, it also increases pressure to accelerate production and infrastructure development. The result is a new version of the global scramble for resources, one in which critical minerals have become strategic assets alongside energy security, industrial policy and geopolitical influence. A new phase of resource nationalism Historically, African debates about mining have focused on ownership, taxation, royalties and local content requirements. Those issues remain important. Increasingly, however, environmental stewardship is becoming part of the resource governance conversation. Countries seeking greater control over mineral wealth may find that environmental performance becomes just as important as revenue generation. Investors, consumers and regulators are placing greater emphasis on sustainability standards, while discussions around deforestation-free supply chains continue to expand. Future mining projects may face growing demands to account not only for direct land disturbance but also for the broader environmental footprint created by associated infrastructure and economic activity. What policymakers can do The study does not argue against mining. Rather, it suggests governments need more sophisticated approaches to managing its environmental consequences. One option is strengthening environmental impact assessments so they capture indirect effects such as road construction, settlement growth and agricultural expansion. Another is improving land-use planning to reduce unnecessary encroachment into sensitive forest areas. Governments could also require stronger forest restoration commitments from mining companies, alongside improved monitoring of deforestation around mining corridors. Expanding local mineral processing may help create greater economic value from extraction, potentially reducing pressure to maximise production volumes at any environmental cost. These measures would not eliminate the trade-offs associated with mining, but they could help narrow the gap between economic development objectives and environmental protection goals. Can development and conservation coexist? The central question raised by the research is not whether Africa should develop its mineral resources. Few policymakers dispute the importance of mining for economic growth, industrialisation and fiscal revenues. Critical minerals present a rare opportunity for many countries to participate more meaningfully in emerging global industries. The challenge is ensuring that this opportunity does not come at the expense of forests that provide equally important long-term value. The University of Sheffield study serves as a reminder that the environmental footprint of mining extends far beyond extraction sites. As demand for transition minerals accelerates, governments, investors and consumers will increasingly be judged on how they manage these broader impacts. Africa’s green future may depend on critical minerals. But the continent’s long-term prosperity will also depend on protecting the forests that sustain its people, biodiversity and climate resilience. The challenge facing African policymakers is no longer whether to exploit critical minerals. It is whether the continent can avoid exchanging one environmental crisis for another. As demand for transition minerals accelerates, Africa may become the testing ground for whether economic development, climate action and environmental protection can genuinely coexist.The post Critical minerals rush puts Africa’s forests at risk first appeared on Africa Briefing.

Keypoints: Kenya and the US are close to a critical minerals agreement The proposed deal prioritises processing minerals within Kenya Ruto says Africa must move beyond exporting raw materials KENYA and the United States are nearing a critical minerals deal that would require strategic resources to be processed locally, as African governments push to capture more value from their natural wealth. The proposed agreement reflects a broader shift in African mining policy. As global demand for critical minerals rises, governments across the continent are increasingly tying resource access to local processing, manufacturing and job creation rather than exporting raw materials. This trend mirrors the growing emphasis on Africa’s critical minerals alliances, as countries seek greater control over strategic resources and downstream industries. ‘Value addition at centre of talks’ Speaking on the sidelines of the G7 summit in France, President William Ruto said negotiations with Washington had reached an advanced stage and could soon result in a formal agreement covering rare earths and other critical minerals. According to Ruto, both sides have agreed in principle that minerals extracted in Kenya should undergo processing locally before export, ensuring that more economic value remains within the country. Ruto said both governments agreed that minerals extracted in Kenya should be processed locally to maximise economic benefits and support industrial development, underscoring Nairobi’s determination to secure greater returns from its natural resources. The comments were reported by Reuters. ‘Africa seeks bigger share of mineral wealth’ The discussions highlight a broader shift in African resource policy. For decades, many African countries exported unprocessed commodities while refining, manufacturing and higher-value activities were concentrated outside the continent. Increasingly, governments are seeking to reverse that model through local content requirements, beneficiation policies and industrial investment commitments. The strategy has gained traction across several resource-rich economies. Zambia has placed renewed emphasis on developing downstream copper industries, while Zimbabwe has introduced measures to encourage domestic lithium processing. The Democratic Republic of Congo has also promoted initiatives aimed at building regional battery and mineral value chains. Across the continent, governments are increasingly following the pattern examined in Africa Briefing’s reporting on African governments tightening control over critical minerals to secure greater domestic economic benefits. ‘US looks to diversify supply chains’ The negotiations also come amid intensifying global competition for critical minerals used in electric vehicles, renewable energy systems, semiconductors and advanced defence technologies. The United States and its allies have accelerated efforts to diversify supply chains and reduce dependence on dominant processing hubs, particularly in China. Critical minerals have become a strategic priority for Western governments seeking secure and resilient access to materials essential for the energy transition. The broader geopolitical implications were explored in Africa Briefing’s analysis of how Africa’s critical minerals are reshaping global power dynamics amid growing competition between major economies. Kenya possesses deposits of several minerals considered important for future industrial and technological applications, including graphite, niobium, copper, nickel and rare earth elements. For Washington, partnerships with African producers offer an opportunity to broaden supply sources. For African governments, they present leverage to negotiate investment terms that support domestic industrialisation. ‘Investment over aid’ Ruto used the G7 gathering to advocate a broader shift in Africa’s engagement with international partners. He argued that the continent is seeking investment-led partnerships focused on industrial growth and job creation rather than relationships centred primarily on aid or resource extraction. According to the Kenyan leader, Africa does not want to be forced to choose between competing global powers. Instead, countries are looking for arrangements that support national development priorities while strengthening their role in global value chains. The comments come as Kenya continues to deepen economic ties with multiple partners, including the United States and China, reflecting a strategy of diversified international engagement. ‘A test case for African industrialisation’ If concluded, the agreement would place Kenya among a growing group of African countries seeking to move beyond extraction and into higher-value mineral processing. Similar ambitions are emerging elsewhere on the continent, including Ghana’s drive to process all minerals locally by 2030, highlighting a wider push to capture more value from natural resources. As competition for critical minerals intensifies, African governments are increasingly insisting that access to their resources must support industrialisation at home. The Kenya-US negotiations could become an early test of whether that strategy delivers tangible economic gains.The post Kenya, US near critical minerals deal with local processing first appeared on Africa Briefing.

Keypoints: President Ruto has invited Arsenal to visit Kenya next year The invitation followed widespread celebrations after Arsenal’s title win Kenya is increasingly using sport to boost tourism and international visibility PRESIDENT William Ruto has invited English champions Arsenal to visit Kenya next year after thousands of supporters celebrated the club’s Premier League title victory across the country. According to Reuters, Ruto said he had instructed officials to extend a formal invitation to Arsenal following scenes of jubilation in Kenyan towns and cities after the club secured its first league title in more than two decades. ‘Arsenal finally closed the gap and it was a huge celebration. I was shocked in Nairobi,’ Ruto told Reuters at the G7 summit in France. ‘It was a big celebration and I am trying to see whether sometime next year Arsenal can come to Kenya.’ Football success sparks diplomatic opportunity The invitation reflects a growing trend among African governments to use sport as a vehicle for tourism promotion, international engagement and national branding. While the immediate trigger was Arsenal’s title success, Kenyan officials also recognise the broader visibility that comes with hosting one of the world’s most recognised football clubs. A visit by Arsenal would attract international media attention while showcasing Kenya’s tourism potential and growing sports sector. Football remains one of the most followed sports across Africa, with millions of supporters maintaining strong ties to leading European clubs through television, digital platforms and supporters’ groups. Thousands celebrate Arsenal triumph Videos shared on social media showed Arsenal supporters gathering in several Kenyan communities to celebrate the club’s title success. Fans waved flags, sang club songs and organised street celebrations that continued late into the night. Reuters reported that Ruto expressed surprise at the scale of the celebrations before deciding to invite the club to visit the country. Thousands of supporters dressed in Arsenal’s red and white colours flooded parts of Nairobi after the club secured the title, illustrating the depth of support the North London side enjoys in Kenya and across East Africa. The scenes underscored the influence European football enjoys across Africa, where Premier League matches regularly attract some of the largest television audiences on the continent. Arsenal’s support base extends well beyond Kenya. The club enjoys significant followings in countries including Ghana, Nigeria, Uganda and Tanzania, reflecting the Premier League’s enduring appeal among African audiences. Across Africa, Premier League clubs enjoy some of their largest international audiences. Broadcasters, sponsors and commercial partners increasingly view the continent as a strategic growth market, helping explain why major European teams are paying closer attention to African supporters and investing more heavily in fan engagement initiatives. Sport and tourism increasingly intertwined Kenya has long leveraged sport to raise its international profile. The country is globally recognised for producing elite long-distance runners and regularly hosts international athletics competitions that attract athletes, visitors and media organisations from around the world. Kenya has also hosted major rugby tournaments and regional sporting events as part of wider efforts to strengthen its tourism sector. Industry analysts increasingly view sport as an effective tourism driver. International sporting events and high-profile team visits can generate hotel bookings, local spending, media coverage and long-term destination awareness. A visit by Arsenal would likely draw interest from supporters across East Africa, creating opportunities for tourism operators, hospitality businesses and local organisers. Africa remains crucial for global football For Europe’s biggest clubs, Africa represents one of the sport’s most important growth markets. The continent’s youthful population, expanding digital connectivity and growing consumer base have helped strengthen football’s commercial appeal. Clubs increasingly engage African supporters through fan events, youth development programmes, digital campaigns and commercial partnerships. A potential Arsenal visit would offer an opportunity to deepen engagement with supporters in one of the club’s most enthusiastic overseas markets while showcasing Kenya to a global audience. Such visits often include coaching clinics, community outreach initiatives, youth football activities and commercial engagements designed to strengthen relationships between clubs and local communities. What happens next? Whether Arsenal accepts the invitation remains uncertain. The club’s calendar is typically crowded with domestic competitions, European commitments and pre-season tours, making scheduling a visit challenging. However, the scale of support demonstrated by Kenyan fans could strengthen the case for future engagement in East Africa. ‘I have sent an invitation because I think it would be a great moment for Arsenal to come to Kenya. They have great fans,’ Ruto told Reuters. For Kenya, the invitation represents more than a football gesture. It reflects an effort to harness the global appeal of sport to support tourism, build international connections and strengthen the country’s visibility on the global stage.The post Ruto invites Arsenal to Kenya after title win first appeared on Africa Briefing.

GENERAL CONTEXT

Haut‑Mbomou Prefecture – South‑East

• On 13 June, a team of 10 staff from a humanitarian organization was intercepted by armed men along the Zémio–Mboki road, between Tamboura and Zébérou, while returning from a mission to implement a capacity-building project for participants in a food security program, funded by the Central African Republic Humanitarian Fund (CAR HF). The assailants fired warning shots before seizing personal belongings and fleeing. No injuries were reported. This incident occurred three days after the interception, on 10 June of a humanitarian convoy comprising vehicles from two other organizations on the same route. Eight humanitarian workers were held for several hours, threatened, robbed of their personal belongings and forced to transport the assailants over several kilometers. On 30 May, in the same area, a team of five humanitarian workers was also robbed by armed men along the Zémio–Dembia road while returning from a mission conducted under a gender‑based violence protection project funded by the CAR HF. The assailants took work equipment, motorcycle batteries and personal belongings. Despite a recent lull, the multiplication of attacks, robberies and abductions affecting humanitarian actors and their convoys continues to raise serious concerns about civilian protection and humanitarian access in Zémio, where movements remain highly restricted.

HUMANITARIAN NEEDS AND RESPONSE

title: DR Congo: Ebola Outbreak, DRC and Region, Situation Report #7, June 18, 2026
summary:
Country: Democratic Republic of the Congo
Source: International Medical Corps

Please refer to the attached file.

FAST FACTS

  • On May 15, the DRC officially declared an outbreak of Ebola virus disease (EVD), later to be confirmed as the Bundibugyo strain.
  • As of June 16, 875 confirmed EVD cases and 202 confirmed EVD deaths had been reported in the DRC, with 19 confirmed cases and two confirmed deaths in Uganda.
  • In the DRC, the outbreak remains centered in Ituri province, with cases also confirmed in North Kivu and South Kivu.
  • In Uganda, reported cases remain linked to transmission originating in the DRC, including imported cases and secondary infections among contacts and healthcare workers.
  • In South Sudan, no cases of EVD have been confirmed, but risk of an outbreak remains high due to transient populations and porous borders with the DRC.

OUR RESPONSE

  • Across the region, our teams are providing case management, infection prevention and control, screening and triage, risk communication and community engagement (RCCE), training and preparedness planning.
  • We are supporting 51 facilities in the screening, identification and treatment of EVD.
  • Our supported sites have conducted 1,324 EVD screenings and provided treatment to 109 patients.
  • We have so far trained 177 people on EVD case management, response and prevention.
  • Our RCCE efforts have reached 36,120 people.

With the support of the US Department of State and other donors, International Medical Corps rapid-response teams are actively responding to the outbreak and engaging with ministries of health, key actors and response partners. International Medical Corps, which is active in more than 70 health facilities across the region, has used a hub-and-spoke model since the outbreak was declared to provide case-management support at designated treatment and transit facilities, strengthen infection prevention and control in referring health facilities, conduct screening and triage, support RCCE in surrounding communities and train health workers on EVD response protocols. The organization is operating Ebola Treatment Centers in all three affected provinces in the DRC, as well as transit centers and screening-and-referral units. In Uganda, it is working with a local partner to provide critical services, supplies and training to health staff in affected areas, and conducting RCCE efforts through village health teams. And in South Sudan, where International Medical Corps is the only implementing partner with active capacity for Ebola case management, it has ensured that two infectious-disease units are now capable of treating suspected or confirmed EVD patients.

title: Tchad : webstory - Le parcours d’une famille soudanaise vers la sécurité
summary:
Countries: Chad, Sudan
Source: UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs

Please refer to the attached file.

Le mois dernier, pour la première fois depuis trois ans, des réfugiés soudanais - Zara Ahmat Ibrahim et ses quatre enfants - ont pu dormir sans crainte. Ils disposaient enfin de leur propre abri : une tente individuelle dans le site d’extension d’Arkoum, dans la province de Ouaddaï, à l’Est du Tchad.

« Dieu merci, j’ai trouvé un toit pour mes enfants. Nous allons pouvoir reconstruire notre vie ici », a-t-elle déclaré.

Juste après leur arrivée sur le site, le 13 mai, un travailleur humanitaire avait inscrit un numéro d’identification sur l’abri nouvellement installé qui leur avait été attribué. Pour Zara, ce geste revêtait une importance profonde. C’était désormais un endroit où ses enfants pouvaient dormir sans craindre les coups de feu ni devoir fuir au milieu de la nuit.

L'abri a été fourni par des partenaires humanitaires avec le soutien du Fonds humanitaire pour le Tchad, dans le cadre du Fonds humanitaire régional pour l'Afrique de l'Ouest et l'Afrique centrale, géré par OCHA.

Un long périple vers la sécurité

Pour Zara et sa famille, le chemin vers la sécurité a commencé il y a trois ans, lorsque le conflit a éclaté au Soudan. Zara et ses enfants sont arrivés à Adré - une ville frontalière au Tchad - sans presque rien : quelques vêtements, une couverture pour ses enfants et l’espoir de trouver un refuge.

Pendant près de trois ans, ils ont vécu dans un campement informel près de la frontière entre le Soudan et le Tchad, dans des conditions extrêmement précaires. Les journées étaient marquées par la chaleur, l’attente et l’incertitude. Les nuits, elles étaient souvent remplies de peur mêlée à l’angoisse quant à l’avenir des enfants.

Cependant, le 13 mai 2026 a marqué un tournant dans leur parcours. Zara et ses enfants ont embarqué dans un convoi de réinstallation en direction du site d’extension d’Arkoum. Pour cette mère, ce départ symbolisait bien plus qu’un simple déménagement : il représentait la chance d’un nouveau départ.

Après plusieurs heures de route, les camions sont enfin arrivés à destination. Lorsque les portes se sont ouvertes, Zara a aidé ses enfants à descendre, avec douceur. Malgré la fatigue du voyage, le soulagement se lisait sur leurs visages.

Derrière eux, le chaos de la frontière ; devant eux, un environnement plus sûr où ils pourront progressivement reconstruire leur vie.

Autres formes de soutien

Les équipes humanitaires ont accueilli d’autres familles nouvellement arrivées le même jour. Les partenaires ont distribué des transferts monétaires conditionnels aux nouveaux arrivants pour les aider à s’installer. Ils ont organisé et orienté les personnes vulnérables vers les services de santé et mis en place des mécanismes de protection.

La communauté humanitaire travaille de concert pour garantir une réponse rapide et coordonnée aux besoins les plus urgents.

« Ce site d’extension aménagé est destiné à accueillir les réfugiés provenant du campement informel d’Adré. Nous remercions les donateurs qui ont financé ce Fonds humanitaire régional pour l’Afrique de l’Ouest et l’Afrique centrale permettant la relocalisation des populations. » Chantal Boloia Zengewa, chef de bureau adjointe, OCHA Tchad.

Des besoins croissants

Depuis le début de la guerre en 2023, l’est du Tchad accueille le plus grand nombre de réfugiés de la région. Zara et sa famille font partie des plus de 928 000 réfugiés soudanais au Tchad.
Chaque jour, des réfugiés épuisés par des jours, voire des semaines de déplacement, continuent d’arriver dans les provinces de l’est du Tchad - Ouaddaï, Wadi Fira et Sila - et dans des sites frontaliers tels qu’Adré. Pour faire face à cette situation d’urgence, les partenaires humanitaires, avec le soutien des fonds humanitaires gérés par OCHA, organisent des opérations de relocalisation vers des sites plus sûrs situés plus à l’intérieur des terres.

Cependant, le développement de ces nouvelles zones n’est pas sans difficultés. L’expansion du site d’Arkoum empiète inévitablement sur les terres agricoles et les pâturages appartenant aux communautés d’accueil, créant parfois des tensions locales liées à la perte de ressources.

Des milliers d’autres familles continuent d’attendre une aide vitale, un abri et une chance de reconstruire leur vie. Dans un contexte où les besoins humanitaires restent immenses, la solidarité internationale reste essentielle pour redonner espoir aux personnes les plus vulnérables.

Par Irène Ndilnodji

title: Libya: ICRC Facts and figures, January - December 2025
summary:
Country: Libya
Source: International Committee of the Red Cross

Please refer to the attached file.

Libya in 2025: Standing alongside communities affected by conflict and violence

In 2025, the humanitarian consequences of armed conflict continued to affect communities across Libya. Families remained separated, people searched for answers about missing loved ones, essential services faced increasing pressure, and many communities continued to live with the long-term consequences of conflict.

Throughout the year, the International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC) in Libya worked alongside the Libyan Red Crescent Society (LRCs), authorities, and local partners to respond to humanitarian needs and strengthen essential services across the country.

Whatever the context - whether widely reported or largely forgotten - the ICRC’s approach has remained the same: to stay close to affected communities, alleviate suffering, and uphold the Fundamental Principles of neutrality, impartiality and independence that enable humanitarian action in post-war situations.

Helping families reconnect and supporting families of the missing

Helping families stay connected and find answers when loved ones are missing has remained at the heart of the ICRC’s humanitarian mission in 2025.

In 2025, the ICRC continued its efforts to restore and maintain family links between separated family members, including detainees, unaccompanied minors, and vulnerable adults. Working closely with the LRCs, the ICRC facilitated phone calls, Red Cross Messages (RCMs) to help families reconnect.

The ICRC also continued to act as a neutral intermediary, engaging with representatives from the east and west of Libya to clarify the fate of people missing in relation to the conflict and to support families searching for answers.

Alongside these efforts, the ICRC maintained confidential dialogue with authorities on humanitarian concerns affecting detainees, internally displaced people, and families of missing persons.

Strengthening forensic capacities and supporting the dignified management of the dead

Proper management of the dead and support for families searching for answers remain essential humanitarian priorities.

In 2025, the ICRC continued strengthening Libya’s medico-legal and forensic capacities through training, technical support, and donations of specialized materials.

Training sessions on the management of the dead were conducted in Tripoli and Sabha for personnel from the Criminal Investigation Department (CID), while Human Remain Recovery Team trainings were organized for the Ministry of Interior and CID Benghazi branch.

The ICRC also supported awareness sessions for LRCS volunteers and continued engagement with relevant authorities, including the General Authority for Research and Identification of Missing Persons (GASIMP).

Material donations were provided to several institutions and facilities, including morgues, hospitals, emergency response centers, and forensic departments to strengthen the recovery and management of human remains.

Delivering health care where it is needed most

In 2025, ensuring access to health care has remained a central pillar of the ICRC’s work for people affected by armed conflict, particularly where health systems have been overwhelmed or deprived of essential resources.

The ICRC supported health facilities across Libya through the provision of medicines, consumables, and medical materials. In addition, primary health care centers received regular support, while additional facilities and hospitals benefited from ad-hoc assistance.

In cooperation with the LRCS, the ICRC also supported medical convoys in Kufra and Ubari, providing hundreds of consultations for women, children, and vulnerable communities living in remote areas.

The ICRC further invested in strengthening emergency response capacities through first aid trainings for weapon bearers and LRCS volunteers across Libya.

Efforts also continued to support the digitization of health services through the implementation of ALMANACH, an innovative digital clinical decision-support system currently operating in several health facilities in Tripoli, Benghazi, Al Khoms, and Sirte.

Physical rehabilitation: Regaining independence, improving quality of life

In 2025, the ICRC continued supporting physical rehabilitation centers in Janzour, Misrata, Benghazi, and Abu Salim Hospital in Tripoli. A total of 795 persons with disabilities benefited from services including prosthetics, orthotics, physiotherapy, and walking aids.

The support included technical mentoring, on-the-job training, equipment donations, and prosthetic and orthotic materials, including high-quality imported components.

The ICRC also supported the Libyan Paralympic Committee through training initiatives aimed at improving inclusion and employment opportunities for persons with disabilities.

Despite the closure of the program, its impact remains significant.

Restoring access to water and sanitation services

In many conflict-affected settings, damage to water systems, housing and basic infrastructure has left people without safe living conditions. In 2025, the ICRC has continued to support access to water, sanitation, shelter and essential services in areas where conflict has disrupted daily life.

In close coordination with Libyan authorities and the LRCS, the ICRC supported projects aimed at restoring and improving critical infrastructure across the country.

Projects included the rehabilitation of wastewater pumping stations in Tarhouna and Sirte, improvements to water systems in Benghazi, support to laboratories and maintenance facilities, and strengthening emergency preparedness capacities of local water authorities.

The ICRC also organized specialized trainings for engineers and public employees in crisis management, emergency response, hydraulics, and water system diagnostics to strengthen national expertise and preparedness.

Supporting livelihoods and economic security

Beyond immediate relief, the ICRC Libya has continued in 2025 to support people’s ability to meet their basic needs and sustain themselves amid conflict.

In 2025, vocational trainings supported 573 individuals in developing income-generating skills such as sewing and electrical maintenance, while the Microeconomic Initiatives (MEI) program provided 834 vulnerable individuals with productive grants to help them start or strengthen small businesses and improve their financial autonomy.

Many beneficiaries were conflict-affected households, internally displaced people, or families of missing persons and persons with disabilities. These activities were implemented in close cooperation with local communities, municipalities, and the Libyan Red Crescent Society.

Promoting the respect for international humanitarian law

Promoting understanding and respect for international humanitarian law remains central to the ICRC’s humanitarian mission.

Throughout 2025, the ICRC organized workshops, trainings, and awareness sessions for military officers, government officials, parliamentarians, LRCS volunteers, and media professionals.

Activities focused on the protection of civilians, detainees, journalists, humanitarian reporting, and challenges related to contemporary armed conflicts, while the Libya joined the Global Initiative to Galvanize Political Commitment to International Humanitarian Law in 2025. The International Committee of the Red Cross also continued engaging with authorities and institutions across the country to strengthen awareness and implementation of IHL.

Reducing risks from weapon contamination

Long after fighting subsides, explosive remnants of war continue to threaten civilians. In 2025, weapon contamination has remained a major concern.

The ICRC has supported risk-awareness activities, engaged directly with communities on safe behaviour and worked with authorities and partners to reduce the dangers posed by unexploded ordnance and other explosive hazards. These efforts have helped prevent injuries and deaths and enabled safer access to homes, fields and essential services.

title: Bosnia and Herzegovina: Mine risk education reduces risks and saves lives – but the danger is far from over
summary:
Country: Bosnia and Herzegovina
Source: International Committee of the Red Cross

Thirty years after the armed conflict, landmines and explosive remnants of war still represent a life threating hazard in Bosnia and Herzegovina. For younger generations with no memory of the conflict, the threat is real, but invisible. Mine risk education may be their only warning.

No child should fear the land they walk on

In August 2025, a 19-year-old was killed in Doboj after entering a marked minefield. He was born after the conflict ended. He had no personal memory of why those mines were placed there, or how they remain. His death illustrates the central challenge facing mine safety efforts in Bosnia and Herzegovina today: the people most at risk are increasingly those who know the least about the danger.

Thirty years on from the conflict, around 2% of the country’s land remains contaminated, while 774 square kilometers remain suspected to contain mines, much of it forested, difficult to access, and slow to clear. In the post-conflict period, 1,862 mine incidents were recorded, leaving 625 people killed, others injured.

Reaching those who don’t remember

The Red Cross Society of Bosnia and Herzegovina (RCSBiH) has run a mine risk education program for 30 years reaching more than 40 mine-affected communities including 600,000 schoolchildren with mine risk awareness programs, supported by the ICRC. Throughout these three decades of collaboration, the ICRC has recognized RCSBiH’s extensive reach and its significant achievements on such an important topic.

Through school visits, camps, and door-to-door outreach in rural areas, the programme brings lifesaving information to those most likely to encounter unexploded ordnance: children, farmers, hunters, fishers, returnees, hikers, and forestry workers.

The Bosnia and Herzegovina Mine Action Centre (BHMAC) which partners with RCSBiH on awareness efforts, is equally focused on educating younger audiences.

Progress, but not resolution

More than 80 per cent of once contaminated areas have been cleared, and mine causality numbers have fallen significantly due to sustained education and demining efforts. But the work is getting harder. Terrain along the former conflict lines has changed over decades, making clearance slower and more technically demanding.

For 30 years, the ICRC has supported the mine risk action program run by the Red Cross Society of Bosnia and Herzegovina (RCSBiH), recognizing its extensive reach and significant achievements in addressing this critical issue. However, the complexity of the challenge remains significant. In 2026, Bosnia and Herzegovina requested from the States Parties to the Anti-Personnel Mine Convention a further extension of its demining deadline, currently set for March 2027.

In Doboj, the loss of a young life in 2025 served as a stark reminder of these dangers. The Red Cross in Tuzla Canton launched an initiative to build a house for the boy’s mother, receiving support from citizens, artists, and businesspeople, which allowed construction to begin soon afterward. This act of compassion highlights the resilience and unity of communities in Bosnia and Herzegovina, even as they continue to face the lingering dangers of landmines.

On 4 April 2026, the International Day for Mine Awareness, the RCSBiH held a series of activities in Mostar, attended by the Head of ICRC Delegation in Bosnia and Herzegovina, Jamila Milovic Halilovic, representatives of BHMAC the EU force in Bosnia and Herzegovina (EUFOR), and numerous state officials, marking the dangers of landmines and unexploded ordnance and the continued importance of mine action. The joint Statement from the RCSBiH event, echoes the fact that although the war ended thirty years ago, its consequences have not. It also carries a message of hope:

There is no secure and lasting peace when mines still pose a threat. Therefore, our message is clear: the safety of people must be a priority. Mine action saves lives and enables the recovery of communities.
