title: Turning Debt into Power: Zambia, the AfDB and Africa's New Frontier in Development Finance
summary: Zambia's landmark debt-for-energy conversion may prove to be more than a successful liability management operation. It offers Africa and the wider Global South a new development finance template: transforming sovereign debt pressure into fiscal space, and fiscal space into productive investment. By linking debt optimisation to electricity access, and by placing the African Development Bank at the heart of the transaction, Zambia has opened a promising pathway for countries seeking to reconcile debt sustainability, energy security and inclusive growth.
full_text: Turning Debt into Power: Zambia, the AfDB and Africa's New Frontier in Development Finance Zambia's landmark debt-for-energy conversion may prove to be more than a successful liability management operation. It offers Africa and the wider Global South a new development finance template: transforming sovereign debt pressure into fiscal space, and fiscal space into productive investment. By linking debt optimisation to electricity access, and by placing the African Development Bank at the heart of the transaction, Zambia has opened a promising pathway for countries seeking to reconcile debt sustainability, energy security and inclusive growth. Africa's debt debate has too often been framed in defensive terms: restructuring, rescheduling, fiscal consolidation and creditor negotiations. Zambia's recent debt-for-energy operation offers a different and potentially transformative narrative. It suggests that sovereign debt management, when intelligently structured and anchored in development priorities, can become an instrument not only of fiscal relief, but of productive investment. The Zambian transaction is significant for three reasons. First, it demonstrates that a sovereign liability can be re-engineered to create fiscal space. Second, it links the savings generated by debt management to a clearly identified development objective: strengthening the electricity system. Third, it positions the African Development Bank not merely as a lender, but as a strategic architect of a new generation of African financial solutions. Why Zambia's Transaction Matters At the heart of the operation is Zambia's buyback of part of its external commercial debt, supported by a US$600 million facility from the African Development Bank and complemented by the country's own resources. The transaction is expected to free resources that will be redirected toward electricity infrastructure, including grid resilience and the modernisation of power distribution. For a country where access to reliable electricity remains a central constraint on households, industry, mining, agriculture and services, the economic significance of such an operation goes well beyond balance-sheet management. This is why the Zambian case deserves close attention across Africa and the wider Global South. It shows that debt conversion can be designed not as an accounting exercise, but as a development compact: creditors accept a financially credible operation; the sovereign improves its debt profile; a multilateral development bank provides concessional or favourable financing; and the fiscal space created is committed to an investment programme with measurable social and economic impact. Electricity Access: Africa's Defining Development Constraint The timing could hardly be more relevant. Nearly 600 million Africans still live without access to electricity. Energy poverty is not only a social deficit; it is a structural barrier to industrialisation, digital transformation, agricultural processing, health services, education and job creation. Without reliable and affordable electricity, Africa's demographic dividend will remain underutilised and its productive transformation delayed. This is precisely the ambition behind Mission 300, the joint initiative of the World Bank Group and the African Development Bank Group to connect 300 million Africans to electricity by 2030. But the challenge is not only about mobilising more money. It is about mobilising better money: longer-term capital, lower-cost finance, risk-sharing instruments, stronger utilities, bankable pipelines and credible national energy compacts. A Replicable Model for the Global South? Zambia's operation points to one possible answer. African countries with high-cost external debt, credible reform programmes and well-defined energy investment needs could explore debt-for-development conversions focused on electricity access. Such mechanisms could be used to finance grid expansion, transmission lines, distribution networks, interconnections, mini-grids, storage, hydropower, solar and wind infrastructure, gas-to-power transition assets where appropriate, and the modernisation of national utilities. Over time, and where governance, safety, regulatory and institutional conditions are fully met, these mechanisms could also support feasibility work and preparatory infrastructure for more advanced dispatchable power options, including small modular reactors. SMRs should not be presented as a shortcut for countries lacking nuclear regulatory capacity, technical skills, safety culture or long-term waste management frameworks. But they are increasingly part of the global conversation on reliable, low-carbon baseload electricity. The recent re-engagement of the World Bank Group with the International Atomic Energy Agency on safe, secure and responsible nuclear energy for development confirms that the financing landscape is evolving. Technology-Neutral, Development-Disciplined Finance For Africa, however, the central question is not whether one technology should be favoured over another. The real question is how to finance a balanced, resilient and sovereign energy mix. In some countries, the priority will be distribution networks and off-grid solar. In others, it will be regional interconnections, hydroelectricity, geothermal power, gas-to-power transition assets or battery storage. In a smaller number of countries with the required institutional maturity, nuclear energy and SMRs may become part of the long-term conversation. Debt conversion mechanisms should therefore be technology-neutral but development-disciplined: they should finance what is bankable, transparent, affordable and aligned with national and regional energy strategies. The AfDB as Architect of African Financial Innovation The role of the African Development Bank in the Zambian transaction is particularly instructive. The AfDB brings more than financial resources. It brings credibility, convening power, knowledge of African economies, sectoral expertise and the ability to structure financing in a way that reassures both governments and markets. In this sense, the Bank is helping to redefine the role of African multilateral finance: not only funding projects but reshaping sovereign balance sheets to release resources for growth-enhancing investment. The Zambian operation should also be read in the broader context of Mission 300, the joint initiative led by the African Development Bank Group and the World Bank Group to connect 300 million Africans to electricity by 2030. It shows how sovereign liability management can be aligned with the continent's most urgent infrastructure priority: universal access to reliable and affordable power. Five Conditions for Replication This model could be especially relevant for countries that meet five conditions. First, the country must have a debt instrument that can realistically be bought back, refinanced or restructured on terms that generate measurable savings. Without genuine financial gains, a debt conversion risks becoming a public relations exercise. Second, the savings must be ring-fenced for clearly identified development investments. In the case of electricity, this means projects with credible implementation plans, procurement discipline, measurable outputs and strong monitoring systems. Third, the operation must be anchored in macroeconomic credibility. Debt conversions cannot substitute for sound fiscal policy, credible public financial management or structural reforms. They work best when they reinforce a broader stabilisation and development strategy. Fourth, the participating multilateral institution must play the role of honest broker and technical anchor. This is where institutions such as the African Development Bank, the World Bank, regional development banks and specialised climate or infrastructure funds can add decisive value. Fifth, transparency is essential. The public, creditors and development partners must be able to see how savings are calculated, where the resources are allocated and what development outcomes are achieved. From Reactive Restructuring to Proactive Debt Transformation The broader lesson is clear: Africa should move from reactive debt restructuring to proactive debt transformation. The continent does not merely need debt relief; it needs development-linked debt engineering. Properly designed, debt-for-energy conversions could become part of a wider toolkit that includes blended finance, guarantees, local currency financing, green and sustainability-linked instruments, infrastructure bonds, regional power pools and public-private partnerships. Yet caution is necessary. Not every country is Zambia. Not every debt profile lends itself to a buyback. Not every electricity programme is implementation-ready. And not every conversion will generate sufficient savings to justify the complexity. Poorly designed transactions could create opacity, moral hazard or new contingent liabilities. For that reason, replication must be selective, disciplined and institutionally robust. A New Mandate for African Development Finance Still, the strategic importance of Zambia's example should not be underestimated. It comes at a time when Africa is seeking to reconcile debt sustainability, energy access, climate responsibility and industrial ambition. It also comes at a time when African institutions are increasingly expected to design African solutions to African financing constraints. For African finance ministers, the message is that debt management should be integrated into national development planning. For central banks and regulators, the message is that financial stability and infrastructure investment must be mutually reinforcing. For investors, the message is that credible African sovereigns, supported by strong multilateral partners, can create innovative structures that reduce risk and enhance development impact. For the African Development Bank, the message is that its role as a catalyst of financial innovation is becoming as important as its role as a provider of capital. Conclusion: Debt as a Bridge to Power Zambia has not solved Africa's energy financing challenge. But it has opened an important door. It has shown that a sovereign debt operation can be linked to electricity access, that fiscal space can be transformed into infrastructure investment, and that African multilateral institutions can help turn financial pressure into development opportunity. If carefully adapted, the Zambian model could inspire a new generation of debt-for-development conversions across Africa and the Global South. The ultimate test will not be the elegance of the financial structure, but the number of homes, schools, hospitals, farms, factories and digital enterprises that receive reliable power as a result. Africa's debt should no longer be viewed only as a burden to be managed. Under the right conditions, it can become a bridge to productive transformation. Zambia's experience shows that the bridge can begin with electricity. By Dr Mohamed H'Midouche, Former International Banker and Development Finance Expert

title: China Expands Africa Strategy Through Trade and Industrial Partnerships
summary:
China Africa ties move centre stage as Beijing targets tariff-free trade, supply-chain shifts and South–South growth.

The post China Expands Africa Strategy Through Trade and Industrial Partnerships appeared first on FurtherAfrica.
full_text: China Expands Africa Strategy Through Trade and Industrial Partnerships China Africa ties move centre stage as Beijing targets tariff-free trade, supply-chain shifts and South–South growth. The post China Expands Africa Strategy Through Trade and Industrial Partnerships appeared first on FurtherAfrica. China Africa ties now sit near the centre of a shifting global order, with Beijing casting the continent as a key partner in a more multipolar system shaped by the Global South.   Speaking during China’s annual parliamentary meetings in March, Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi argued that emerging economies, particularly in Africa and the wider Global South, will play an increasingly important role in shaping future global governance and economic growth. For investors, the message is significant. China is no longer approaching Africa primarily as a source of raw materials. Instead, Beijing increasingly views the continent as a strategic partner in manufacturing, logistics, trade and industrial development. Africa becomes a strategic pillar of China’s global agenda China remains Africa’s largest bilateral trading partner, with economic ties now extending well beyond commodities into infrastructure, industrial parks, digital connectivity, manufacturing and logistics. Recent Chinese policy initiatives suggest a growing emphasis on value addition and industrialisation. This aligns with African governments’ efforts to process more resources domestically, develop manufacturing capacity and increase participation in regional and global value chains. Wang Yi’s remarks reinforced Beijing’s long-standing position that developing countries should have a greater voice in global institutions and economic decision-making. Chinese officials continue to present the country’s engagement with Africa as a partnership focused on development, sovereignty and mutual economic growth. Trade remains a central pillar of this strategy. China has announced plans to expand duty-free access for imports from African countries with which it maintains diplomatic relations. While implementation details continue to evolve, the initiative is designed to increase African exports to China and strengthen commercial links across multiple sectors, including agriculture, manufacturing and selected mineral products. For African exporters, improved market access could create new opportunities in sectors where demand from Chinese consumers and manufacturers continues to grow. Supply chains, industrialisation and investment opportunities China’s evolving Africa strategy comes at a time when global supply chains are becoming more diversified and geopolitical tensions are reshaping trade patterns. As companies seek alternative production locations and more resilient sourcing networks, African markets are increasingly attracting attention as potential manufacturing and logistics hubs. China’s growing support for industrial parks, transport corridors and processing industries reflects this shift. Beijing also continues to frame its engagement through broader South-South cooperation platforms, including BRICS and the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation. Chinese policymakers argue that these institutions can complement existing global structures while providing emerging economies with a stronger voice in finance, infrastructure and technology cooperation. For investors, the practical implications are becoming clearer. Future China–Africa engagement is likely to focus less on isolated infrastructure projects and more on integrated economic ecosystems built around trade corridors, manufacturing clusters, logistics networks and digital infrastructure. The success of that approach will depend heavily on how African governments align Chinese investment with national industrialisation strategies and initiatives such as the African Continental Free Trade Area. The next phase of China–Africa ties will therefore be measured not only by trade volumes or infrastructure spending, but by whether new partnerships generate greater value addition, stronger industrial capacity and more competitive export sectors across the continent. For investors, that evolution could create opportunities across manufacturing, logistics, digital services and cross-border trade infrastructure over the coming decade. title: Kenya–US Critical Minerals Deal Advances as Nairobi Pushes Local Processing
summary:
Kenya minerals deal nears finalisation with the US, prioritising in-country processing of rare earths and strategic minerals.

The post Kenya–US Critical Minerals Deal Advances as Nairobi Pushes Local Processing appeared first on FurtherAfrica.
full_text: Kenya–US Critical Minerals Deal Advances as Nairobi Pushes Local Processing Kenya minerals deal nears finalisation with the US, prioritising in-country processing of rare earths and strategic minerals. The post Kenya–US Critical Minerals Deal Advances as Nairobi Pushes Local Processing appeared first on FurtherAfrica. The Kenya minerals deal is advancing rapidly, signalling a new phase in the country’s mining strategy as Nairobi moves closer to a critical minerals agreement with the United States that would prioritise domestic processing of strategic resources.   A strategic deal tied to beneficiation and supply chains Kenyan President William Ruto said talks with the United States on a critical minerals partnership are at an “advanced stage” and could be completed soon. He spoke on the margins of the G7 Summit in France, where he held discussions with leaders including US President Donald Trump. The proposed framework would cover rare earth elements and other strategic minerals used in clean energy and advanced technology industries. Crucially, Ruto said both sides agree that minerals under the partnership should be processed in Kenya rather than exported in raw form. That stance aligns with a broader African policy shift towards local beneficiation. Governments across the continent seek to retain more value from resources that underpin electric vehicles, renewable power systems, battery supply chains and advanced manufacturing. Countries such as the Democratic Republic of the Congo and Zimbabwe have already moved to expand domestic processing capacity and, in some cases, limit exports of unprocessed ores. Kenya now appears ready to anchor a similar strategy in a bilateral deal with the United States, positioning itself as a regional hub for critical mineral processing. For investors, the Kenya minerals deal points to future demand for capital in concentrators, refineries, logistics and power infrastructure needed to support local value addition. Kenya holds known deposits of rare earth minerals and niobium and is exploring for lithium, graphite, copper and nickel, which are considered prospective but remain largely untapped. These resources sit at the centre of global competition over critical minerals security. Western economies are looking to reduce reliance on Chinese processing and refining capacity. G7 leaders recently agreed to strengthen cooperation on supply chains for such materials and diversify processing away from single-country dependence. The proposed Kenya–US accord fits that agenda while also responding to African calls for more balanced economic partnerships. From extraction to investment-led partnerships Ruto framed the talks as part of a wider reset in Africa’s engagement with Western partners, calling for a move away from extractive models built on raw material exports. He argued that natural resources from the continent “can no longer be exported and processed elsewhere” and should instead be processed “in-country and in-continent” to create jobs and industrial capacity. He also said Kenya and its peers will “reject” relationships centred on simple resource extraction. They are looking instead for partnerships that emphasise investment, industrial development and employment creation. That language aligns with a growing push by African leaders to secure deals that lock in commitments on processing, technology transfer and local content. Beyond mining, Ruto linked the Kenya minerals deal to a broader push to change how Africa accesses global capital. He argued that Africa is constrained less by a lack of capital than by weak mechanisms to mobilise existing savings and reduce financing costs. He highlighted the scale of African pension funds, insurance assets and reserves. He argued that these could support more domestic investment if backed by stronger guarantee and risk-sharing tools. Ruto welcomed growing support for African financial institutions, citing the African Trade & Investment Development Insurance (ATIDI), formerly the African Trade Insurance Agency, as a platform that can help lower investment risk and unlock capital flows. If paired with a credible mineral processing strategy, such risk-mitigation capacity could crowd in long-term private investment into Kenyan downstream assets. For investors, the direction of travel is clear. If finalised on the terms outlined by Ruto, the Kenya minerals deal would anchor Kenya’s attempt to become a processing and industrial hub for strategic minerals, with policy support for in-country value addition and a stronger role for African capital. The next signals to watch will be the final structure of the agreement, any linked fiscal or regulatory reforms, and the first wave of concrete processing and refining projects that emerge on the back of the pact. title: Angola tourism finance: Gulf capital eyes niche sector
summary:
Angola tourism finance advances as African Bank of Oman channels Gulf patient capital into niche and mass tourism projects.

full_text: Angola tourism finance: Gulf capital eyes niche sector Angola tourism finance advances as African Bank of Oman channels Gulf patient capital into niche and mass tourism projects. The post Angola tourism finance: Gulf capital eyes niche sector appeared first on FurtherAfrica. Angola tourism finance is gaining new momentum as African Bank of Oman positions itself to channel Gulf patient capital into the country’s underdeveloped tourism sector. African Bank of Oman is seeking to position itself as a bridge for Gulf patient capital into Angola’s underdeveloped tourism sector. This signals a new angle for Angola tourism finance as the country looks beyond oil for growth. Gulf capital looks at Angola’s tourism gap At a media briefing in Luanda themed “Patient Gulf Capital: financing the next frontier of Angolan tourism”, African Bank of Oman (ABO) chief executive António Dinis Mendes argued that tourism in Angola currently accounts for less than 1% of GDP. This underscores how far the sector lags regional peers. He framed this gap as an opportunity, not a constraint, especially for investors willing to take longer-dated bets. Mendes set out a two-step thesis. First, focus on niche tourism segments, which attract higher-spend visitors and require less extensive infrastructure than mass-market tourism. In his view, per-capita spending is higher in niche segments. The associated infrastructure bill is also lower than for large-scale resorts or high-volume coastal developments. As a result, the bank sees niche eco-lodges, high-end safari assets, and targeted cultural or business tourism as the more viable starting point. Second, once core roads, utilities, and hospitality capacity improve, the model could shift towards mass tourism. Here, the cost per tourist is lower but infrastructure needs are far greater. This sequencing matters for Angola tourism finance because it offers institutional investors a phased entry point. Projects start smaller and more contained, but can still scale if policy and infrastructure progress. Mendes stressed that ABO does not aim to compete with local commercial lenders. Instead, it aims to structure and channel patient capital from the Gulf in partnership with Angolan commercial and development banks, as well as the country’s sovereign wealth fund. The bank is positioning itself as an arranger and connector, matching Gulf investors’ capital with bankable tourism assets in Angola. Cassava platform and the Gulf–Africa corridor ABO highlighted that Gulf states invested about US$179 billion in Africa between 2012 and 2025. This underlines a growing pipeline of capital already familiar with African risk. Within this broader flow, ABO pointed to a specific tourism and real estate investment platform, the Cassava Fund, which is backed by Qatari interests. Cassava has already deployed around US$500 million into Rwanda, focused on real estate and tourism-related assets. According to Mendes, the fund has a further US$500 million earmarked for Angola, contingent on the presentation of sustainable, well-structured projects. The bank described this as part of a wider Gulf line for Africa that exceeds US$500 million, rather than a one-off commitment. In practice, ABO expects to act as a gateway. Through its shareholder base and Gulf relationships, it can identify regional investors and specialist tourism operators, then syndicate deals alongside Angolan and regional financiers. Operators would run the underlying assets, while funds like Cassava would provide equity or quasi-equity. Local banks and development institutions could then supply complementary debt. During the briefing, Mendes also drew parallels with Oman’s own trajectory. The Gulf state, with a GDP similar in scale to Angola’s in dollar terms, spent years highly dependent on oil and gas. It then embarked on a privatisation and diversification programme. Over roughly five years, this shift supported rapid expansion in agriculture and tourism. The implication for investors is clear: Angola’s resource dependence is not structurally unique, and tourism can become a meaningful pillar if reforms and capital align. For institutional investors, the signal is that Angola tourism finance is moving from concept to structured platforms backed by Gulf capital. The immediate focus will be whether ABO can bring credible, sustainable projects to close, turning indicated lines from Cassava and other Gulf players into executed transactions that test Angola’s tourism thesis at scale. title: Sub-Saharan Africa Leads Global Energy Transition
summary:
Africa energy transition gains momentum as Sub-Saharan Africa tops WEF 2026 Index gains. What it means for investors.

The post Sub-Saharan Africa Leads Global Energy Transition appeared first on FurtherAfrica.
full_text: Sub-Saharan Africa Leads Global Energy Transition Africa energy transition gains momentum as Sub-Saharan Africa tops WEF 2026 Index gains. What it means for investors. The post Sub-Saharan Africa Leads Global Energy Transition appeared first on FurtherAfrica. Sub-Saharan Africa is emerging as one of the clearest outperformers in the Africa energy transition, just as global progress loses momentum.   According to the World Economic Forum‘s Energy Transition Index 2026, the region recorded the strongest gains of any geography worldwide, even as overall transition readiness fell for the first time in more than a decade. A fractured transition with Africa as an outlier The WEF’s latest Energy Transition Index tracks 120 countries across 44 indicators, covering system performance and readiness for cleaner, more secure and affordable energy. The 2026 edition shows a notable setback: transition readiness declined, with four of the five enabling dimensions weakening at the same time. Those dimensions include regulation, infrastructure, capital, innovation and human capital. This reversal comes despite record global capital deployment. The report estimates US$3.3 trillion in total energy investment in 2025, of which US$2.3 trillion went into clean energy technologies and infrastructure. Yet that investment has not translated into broad-based gains in readiness, highlighting structural bottlenecks rather than a lack of capital at the system level. The WEF notes that the global shift is now shaped by tighter geopolitics, higher electricity demand, grid and permitting bottlenecks, and unequal access to finance. Emerging economies, many of them in Africa, now account for about 80% of global electricity demand growth, driven by economic expansion, urbanisation, digital infrastructure and rising access needs. However, about three-quarters of global clean energy investment still flows to a relatively small group of countries, leaving a widening gap between where capital is deployed and where demand is growing fastest. This is the core risk — and opportunity — around the Africa energy transition. Against this backdrop, Sub-Saharan Africa stands out. The region delivered the strongest gains of any region in the index, even as Latin America and the Middle East and North Africa recorded setbacks linked to weaker policies, softer infrastructure spending and lower readiness. The WEF highlights expanding renewable projects, efforts to increase electricity access and policy moves to attract investment as key drivers of the region’s score improvement. Roberto Bocca, head of the WEF Centre for Energy and Materials, argues the transition “is not reversing, but it is fracturing,” with security, affordability and resilience now central to sustaining progress. Recent disruptions in strategic chokepoints such as the Strait of Hormuz underscore how exposed import-dependent emerging markets remain to supply shocks and price volatility. Where demand, infrastructure and capital needs converge For investors, the signal is clear. Sub-Saharan Africa is becoming one of the few markets where rising electricity demand, infrastructure build-out and capital needs align into a visible, long-term pipeline. The region’s outperformance on the Energy Transition Index does not reflect a high absolute base. Rather, it reflects meaningful progress from a constrained starting point, driven by governments that increasingly view renewables and grids as growth enablers. The WEF identifies three priorities to sustain and monetise this progress: integrating energy security and resilience into system design; accelerating grid expansion and wider infrastructure; and improving investment conditions through stable policy and targeted capital flows. These are all areas where private and development finance can play complementary roles. The capital allocation imbalance is particularly relevant. With 80% of incremental electricity demand coming from emerging markets but only about 25% of clean-energy capital reaching them, there is structural room for more risk-tolerant capital, blended finance and local-currency solutions in Africa. Grid investments, storage, flexible generation and digital infrastructure around distribution and metering all present scalable opportunities tied to the Africa energy transition. The WEF report concludes that countries able to strengthen resilience, expand infrastructure and attract investment will convert today’s pressures into long-term economic and competitive gains. For institutional investors and financiers, Sub-Saharan Africa’s recent performance suggests the region is moving into that category. The next phase will hinge on whether policy reforms, grid build-out and new capital structures can turn index gains into bankable projects at scale — an arc that will define the investable frontier of the Africa energy transition over the coming decade. Angola energy reform gets the big-screen treatment in a new documentary pitching African upstream to global capital.

The post Angola Energy Reform Takes Centre Stage in New Investor-Focused Documentary appeared first on FurtherAfrica. Angola energy reform is moving from policy papers to the big screen, as a new feature documentary turns a decade of oil-sector transformation into an investor-facing visual case study.   Angola’s story of structural change is set to reach a wider investment audience. A new feature documentary turns Angola energy reform into a visual case study of how policy, governance and local enterprise helped stabilise oil output at around one million barrels per day. From book to investor-facing film Global production house Soyini Tales Inc., led by founder Tahira Francis, has started work on a premium feature documentary based on NJ Ayuk’s book Crude Oil: Power, Turnaround and Transformation in Angola. Filming is due to begin next week in Angola and will include interviews, site visits and on-the-ground documentation across key energy and economic locations. The film follows a ten-year narrative arc. It traces Angola’s shift from an oil-fuelled boom through a period of sharp macroeconomic contraction, and into the current phase of reform-driven recovery in the energy sector. The project aims to show how a combination of regulatory overhaul, institutional reform and market discipline helped the country maintain crude production at about one million barrels per day. That level now anchors Angola’s role in African upstream supply. Unlike traditional policy reviews, the documentary is framed through the experiences of three generations of Angolans. It links boardroom decisions and regulatory changes to outcomes in oilfields and households. This positions Angola energy reform as both a macroeconomic story and a social one. The producers plan a distribution strategy across the United States, Europe and major digital streaming platforms. They explicitly pitch the film as an investor-facing visual reference for those tracking African energy transitions and upstream flows. Reform architects and local value capture The documentary will spotlight the country’s main reform architects. It highlights the political direction set by President João Lourenço. It covers the commercial discipline brought to national oil company Sonangol by chief executive Sebastião Gaspar Martins. It also examines the regulatory overhaul driven by Paulino Jerónimo at the National Agency for Petroleum, Gas and Biofuels (ANPG), Angola’s national concessionaire. Together, these institutions rewrote the rules for licensing, operations and market engagement. They helped restore investor confidence in Angola’s offshore and onshore prospects. The film also brings a sharper focus on local content. It showcases João Filipe at Cabship, active in marine logistics and cargo management for offshore operations. It follows Janice Faria at Enagol, which provides upstream engineering and fuel services. It profiles Francisco Monteiro at Brimont, working in procurement and chemical supply. It features Bráulio de Brito at Tradinter, whose oilfield consulting and business advocacy support project development. These case studies underline how local firms are capturing and retaining more value within Angola’s modernising energy economy. For NJ Ayuk — who has written several books on African energy economics — this is the first time one of his works is adapted into a feature documentary. Producer Tahira Francis describes Angola’s experience as a powerful blueprint of resilience. She argues it shows how countries can build true economic sovereignty by backing domestic visionaries and reformers. For investors, the film arrives as interest in African upstream assets is being recalibrated in light of energy transition pressures and capital discipline. By putting Angola energy reform on screen, the documentary could shape how global capital allocates to Angolan and wider African projects over the next decade. This is especially relevant if the country sustains its one-million-barrel-per-day benchmark and continues to deepen local participation in the value chain. Investors and executives tracking African upstream should watch whether the film’s distribution reach translates into measurable capital inflows to Angola’s oil sector through 2026 and beyond. title: India Apple Market Puts South Africa’s Trade Strategy to the Test
summary:
India apple market demand surges, but a 50% tariff gap threatens South African exporters as rivals secure preferential access.

The post India Apple Market Puts South Africa’s Trade Strategy to the Test appeared first on FurtherAfrica.
full_text: India Apple Market Puts South Africa’s Trade Strategy to the Test India apple market demand surges, but a 50% tariff gap threatens South African exporters as rivals secure preferential access. The post India Apple Market Puts South Africa’s Trade Strategy to the Test appeared first on FurtherAfrica. The India apple market has become a strategic prize for South African exporters — but a widening tariff gap now threatens to turn that opportunity into a test of trade diplomacy.   South Africa’s fast-growing demand for imported apples has made the India apple market a top target for its exporters. Now a widening tariff gap threatens to turn that prize into a test of South Africa’s trade diplomacy and the sector’s long-term competitiveness. Strong brands, stronger demand South African exporters have built a meaningful presence in India’s imported fruit segment, anchored in apples and pears. Indian importers report that South African fruit has a clear reputation for quality, consistency and value for money, especially in high-coloured Gala varieties. Mumbai-based NGK Trading illustrates the depth of that footprint. The company imports about 300 containers of South African fruit a year, including roughly 220 containers of apples and pears. Owner Gagan Khosla notes that South African apples have established themselves well in India and highlights Royal Gala as a core favourite, with Flash Gala gaining ground each season as awareness grows. For Tru-Cape Fruit Marketing, India has become one of its most important offshore growth markets. The company exported more than 650,000 MK6-equivalent cartons of apples and pears to India in 2025. Management sees particular upside in premium Flash Gala, which aligns well with India’s rising demand for visually appealing, sweeter fruit. This demand is underpinned by a rapidly expanding urban middle class and a clear shift towards premium imported produce. As household incomes rise and modern retail expands, imported apples have moved from a niche category to a regular feature in many urban baskets. That structural trend positions India as one of the most attractive long-term growth avenues for South African pome fruit exporters. Tariff gap now the critical risk The challenge is that this commercial success is colliding with an increasingly adverse tariff regime. South African apples and pears currently enter India facing a 50% import duty. That headline rate already compresses margins and forces exporters and importers to work hard on efficiency to keep landed prices competitive. However, India is now cutting tariffs for key rivals. According to importers, tariffs on apples from Europe are set to fall to 20%, while New Zealand will benefit from a 25% tariff from January 2027. Chile is also in talks with India to reduce its duty on apples. If agreed, these deals will leave South Africa at a 25–30 percentage point disadvantage on price before logistics, branding or in-market spend are considered. Tru-Cape managing director Roelf Pienaar is blunt about the risk. He argues that if competitors gain significantly better tariff access while South Africa remains at 50%, it will become progressively more difficult to compete on price, regardless of product quality. In other words, the product story is strong but cannot indefinitely outweigh a structural tax headwind. Riaan Ferreira, director of GF Marketing, which partners Tru-Cape in India and other export markets, frames the issue as a trade policy priority. India has tremendous potential for South African fruit, he says, but South Africa needs a broader, more preferential trade agreement with India to maintain and grow its position. Once lower tariffs fully apply to rival origins, he expects South Africa’s competitive position to come under pressure, as quality alone cannot offset a 25–30 percentage point tariff gap. For investors and lenders across South Africa’s fruit value chain, the stakes are clear. Export revenue growth, varietal investment decisions and packhouse and cold-chain capital allocation increasingly depend on whether South Africa can secure improved access to the India apple market. If policymakers deliver a preferential trade deal, India can remain a high-growth, margin-accretive outlet for South African apples and pears. If not, producers may need to rebalance towards other markets, focus harder on ultra-premium varieties, or accept thinner margins in India. Over the next few years, tariff negotiations between Pretoria and New Delhi, the pace of India’s middle-class expansion and the response of competing suppliers will shape that outcome. Investors should track these trade talks closely, alongside shipment volumes of Royal Gala and Flash Gala into India, as forward indicators of where pricing power and capital returns in South Africa’s apple industry are heading. Keypoints Accra hosted the ‘Next Step’ conference on reparatory justice President Mahama reaffirmed Ghana’s support for reparations African and Caribbean leaders sought practical pathways for action AFRICAN and Caribbean leaders have moved to advance a coordinated global reparations campaign during the Next Step: High-Level Consultative Conference on Reparatory Justice, where Barbados Prime Minister Mia Mottley unveiled an expanded reparations manifesto and Ghana reaffirmed its commitment to the movement. The gathering brought together political leaders, legal experts, academics and civil society representatives to discuss how recent international momentum, including the Ghana-backed UN resolution on slavery justice, can be translated into practical action on reparatory justice. Reparations movement enters new phase The June 18-19 conference reflects a growing alliance between African and Caribbean governments seeking reparatory justice for the transatlantic slave trade and colonialism. Supporters argue that the movement has entered a new phase following the UN resolution and increased international attention to historical injustices, while critics continue to question the legal basis, practical implementation and financial implications of compensation claims. Organisers described the gathering as a ‘Next Step’ conference aimed at moving discussions on reparatory justice beyond declarations and symbolic recognition towards practical frameworks for implementation. Discussions focused on diplomacy, legal mechanisms, historical accountability, development financing and international cooperation between Africa and the Caribbean. The discussions also built upon the Caribbean Community’s Ten-Point Plan for Reparatory Justice, which has served as a foundation for regional advocacy on reparations for more than a decade. During the summit, Mottley unveiled a revised reparations framework that expands earlier Caribbean proposals to include the impact of slavery on women and girls, Indigenous communities and countries facing climate-related vulnerabilities. The document argues that reparations should move beyond symbolic recognition and include investment in education, healthcare, economic development, cultural restoration and climate resilience. It also reiterates calls for formal apologies and compensation from governments, institutions, religious organisations and commercial entities that benefited from slavery. ‘Next Step’ conference seeks practical action The ‘Next Step: High-Level Consultative Conference on Reparatory Justice’ has become one of the most significant international gatherings on the issue since the adoption of the UN resolution earlier this year. Delegates from dozens of countries attended discussions on how political commitments can be transformed into actionable policies and international frameworks. Participants examined legal pathways, development financing mechanisms, educational initiatives and cultural restoration programmes that could form part of a broader reparatory justice agenda. A recurring message throughout the conference was the need to shift the debate from recognition to action. Speakers emphasised that the challenge is no longer establishing the historical record of slavery and colonial exploitation, but developing practical mechanisms capable of addressing their enduring consequences. The conference also highlighted growing cooperation between African governments and Caribbean states, with leaders emphasising the importance of presenting a coordinated position in international forums. Mahama backs expanded reparations agenda Ghanaian President John Dramani Mahama used the conference to reaffirm support for reparatory justice, reinforcing Ghana’s position as one of the leading African advocates for the movement. Mahama, who serves as the African Union’s reparations champion, has argued that the transatlantic slave trade and colonial exploitation continue to shape global inequalities and require meaningful international engagement. Speaking at the conference, Mahama said reparatory justice was not solely about addressing historical grievances but also about confronting contemporary inequalities rooted in centuries of exploitation and exclusion, arguing that the legacy of slavery continues to shape global economic disparities. His participation alongside Caribbean leaders such as Mottley underscored the growing convergence between African and Caribbean governments on the issue. Organisers said the conference was intended to transform recent diplomatic momentum into practical institutional frameworks capable of advancing reparatory justice worldwide. Mahama has previously described the transatlantic slave trade as ‘the greatest crime against humanity ever perpetrated’ and has called for a coordinated continental effort to pursue reparatory justice through diplomacy, historical accountability and international dialogue. For many African policymakers, the debate extends beyond historical acknowledgement. Advocates argue that the economic consequences of slavery and colonialism continue to shape patterns of inequality, underdevelopment and global wealth distribution. Calls for compensation face political hurdles The expanded reparations agenda arrives amid growing pressure on European governments to engage more directly with reparations debates. However, significant political and legal obstacles remain. Successive British governments have expressed regret over Britain’s role in the slave trade but have stopped short of supporting direct financial reparations. Other European governments have adopted similar positions, favouring development partnerships and educational initiatives over compensation programmes. Critics of reparations proposals argue that assigning financial liability across generations presents major legal and practical challenges. They also question how compensation would be calculated, distributed and administered across affected countries and communities. Supporters counter that international law increasingly recognises historical injustices and that reparatory justice can take multiple forms, including debt relief, development financing, institutional reform, educational investment and cultural restitution. Economic questions remain unresolved One of the most contentious aspects of the reparations debate concerns scale and implementation. While researchers and advocacy groups have attempted to estimate the economic impact of slavery and colonial exploitation, there is no internationally agreed mechanism for calculating compensation. Some academic studies have estimated that the value of labour, resources and wealth extracted through slavery and colonial systems amounts to trillions of dollars, although methodologies and conclusions vary significantly across different research projects. Recent research has strengthened calls for structured negotiations between former colonial powers and countries seeking reparatory measures, while also raising questions about whether reparations can translate into tangible outcomes for affected communities. Yet many observers acknowledge that any future settlement is likely to involve a combination of financial and non-financial measures rather than direct cash payments alone. Africa-Caribbean partnership gains momentum Perhaps the most significant outcome of the Accra gathering is the strengthening relationship between African and Caribbean nations on issues of historical justice. Delegates argued that reparatory justice encompasses a broad range of measures, including education, healthcare, cultural restoration, historical recognition and policies aimed at addressing inequalities rooted in slavery and colonialism. The conference reflects a wider push by the African Union and CARICOM to elevate reparations from a moral argument into a structured diplomatic agenda. Advocates believe the growing coordination between African and Caribbean governments could increase pressure on former colonial powers to engage more substantively with demands for restorative justice. Whether governments in Europe and North America engage with the expanded demands remains uncertain. However, participants said the Accra conference demonstrated that reparations have moved from the margins of international diplomacy towards the centre of debates over historical justice, development financing and global inequality. Keypoints: Ghana launches three global reparations panels Mahama says world must move from recognition to action New bodies will focus on justice, artefact restitution and legal pathways GHANA has established three new international panels on reparatory justice, cultural restitution and legal redress as President John Mahama seeks to move the global slavery reparations campaign from diplomatic recognition to implementation. The announcement, made during the opening of the Next Step: High-Level Consultative Conference in Accra on June 18, represents the most significant institutional step since the United Nations General Assembly adopted Resolution A/RES/80/250 in March following Ghana’s campaign for a UN vote on slavery reparations. Ghana now hopes to transform that diplomatic breakthrough into a practical international framework capable of advancing reparatory justice worldwide. The issue has gained momentum in recent years as African and Caribbean governments have intensified calls for formal acknowledgement of slavery’s lasting economic and social consequences. At the same time, international debates over cultural restitution, historical accountability and the return of colonial-era artefacts have moved increasingly into mainstream diplomatic discussions. Speaking before heads of state, government officials, scholars, legal experts and representatives of the African diaspora, Mahama said the global conversation must now shift from acknowledgement of historical injustices to concrete action. Three new bodies to drive implementation At the centre of the announcement was the creation of three international panels designed to support the next phase of the reparations movement. The first, a Global Advisory Panel on Reparatory Justice, will bring together current and former heads of state, eminent international figures and policymakers to provide strategic direction and promote international cooperation. The second, an Expert Panel on the Restitution of Cultural Artefacts, will focus on facilitating the return of cultural artefacts, archives, sacred objects and historical treasures removed from Africa and other affected communities. The third, a Global Legal Panel on Reparatory Justice, will assemble jurists and legal scholars to examine potential legal avenues under international law, including restitution, institutional accountability and other forms of reparatory justice. Together, the three bodies are intended to provide the political leadership, legal expertise and technical support that advocates say have been missing from previous reparations initiatives. ‘We must move from recognition to building the architecture for reparatory justice,’ Mahama told delegates. He stressed that the panels were not intended to replace governments, regional organisations or international institutions but rather to strengthen their work through technical expertise, policy guidance and legal analysis. UN resolution enters new phase The conference comes less than three months after the UN General Assembly adopted Resolution A/RES/80/250 with the backing of 123 member states, marking a major diplomatic victory for Ghana and its partners. Mahama described the vote as an important milestone but argued that the real challenge now lies in translating international recognition into measurable outcomes. ‘The responsibility now is to ensure that this recognition translates into meaningful and sustained action,’ he said. According to the President, the consequences of slavery and racialised chattel enslavement continue to shape global inequalities, institutions and economic structures centuries after the practice formally ended. ‘History does not ask us to inherit guilt, but it asks us to inherit responsibility,’ he said. That message formed a central theme of his address, with Mahama seeking to frame reparatory justice not as an exercise in assigning blame to present generations but as an effort to address enduring historical consequences. Africa and Caribbean deepen cooperation The Accra conference also highlighted growing cooperation between Africa and the Caribbean on reparations. The meeting builds on Africa-Caribbean coordination on reparations, which has increasingly transformed the issue from an advocacy campaign into a structured diplomatic initiative. Mahama endorsed the African Union’s decision to establish an African-Caribbean Joint Mechanism on Reparative Justice and praised decades of advocacy by African governments, CARICOM member states, civil society organisations, legal experts and diaspora groups. The African Union declared reparations a major continental priority in 2025 and appointed Mahama as the AU Champion on Reparations, placing Ghana at the forefront of efforts to coordinate Africa’s position on the issue. The move also aligns with the broader African Union campaign for reparations, which has gained momentum across the continent over the past year. Caribbean nations have long pursued reparatory justice through the CARICOM Reparations Commission, which has advocated measures ranging from formal apologies and educational programmes to economic development initiatives and cultural restoration. Mahama argued that because the slave trade connected Africa, the Caribbean, North America and South America through a shared history, any meaningful response must be similarly international in scope. ‘The search for justice must therefore be transcontinental in its ambition,’ he said. Support grows but debate remains The reparations movement has gained visibility in recent years, with religious institutions, universities and governments increasingly examining their historical links to slavery. During his speech, Mahama welcomed engagement from institutions including the Vatican, the Church of England and the Church of Scotland, as well as comments from French President Emmanuel Macron on historical justice. However, the issue remains politically sensitive. While support for reparatory justice has grown across Africa and the Caribbean, several Western governments continue to reject direct financial compensation, arguing that present-day states should not be held legally liable for actions committed centuries ago. Mahama sought to address those concerns by emphasising responsibility rather than blame and by advocating dialogue, partnership and shared commitment to human dignity. Cultural restitution gains momentum One of the most significant practical elements of the initiative is the focus on cultural restitution. Calls for the return of African artefacts held in museums and private collections across Europe and North America have intensified in recent years, with several governments and institutions beginning to review historical acquisitions. The debate has gathered pace as European governments consider new approaches to France’s proposed artefact return legislation and wider restitution efforts. The newly announced expert panel will seek to support and accelerate those efforts by providing expertise and facilitating engagement between countries, museums, researchers and cultural institutions. Observers view cultural restitution as one of the areas where tangible progress may be achievable in the near term, even as broader debates over reparations and compensation continue. Building a post-adoption framework The Accra gathering is the first major international conference convened since the UN resolution was adopted and is expected to help shape the next phase of the global reparations movement. Delegates are examining a draft post-adoption framework intended to guide future cooperation on truth-telling, education, memorialisation, cultural restitution, research and legal remedies. Mahama also emphasised the importance of including the African diaspora in decision-making, describing descendants of enslaved Africans as rights holders whose experiences and aspirations must help shape future initiatives. The President said future generations would judge today’s leaders not by the resolutions they adopted but by the progress they achieved. For Ghana, the objective is clear: to ensure that a historic diplomatic victory at the United Nations becomes the foundation for sustained international action. The success of the initiative will likely depend on whether governments, international institutions and former colonial powers are willing to engage with recommendations that emerge from the new panels in the months ahead. The outcome could significantly influence the future direction of the broader global reparations debate.The post Ghana launches three global reparations panels first appeared on Africa Briefing.

Keypoints: Namibia linked genocide negotiations with Germany to Africa’s wider reparations campaign President Netumbo Nandi-Ndaitwah backed implementation of a landmark UN resolution on reparatory justice Namibia highlighted its new national Genocide Remembrance Day initiative NAMIBIAN President Netumbo Nandi-Ndaitwah has linked Namibia’s genocide negotiations with Germany to Africa’s expanding campaign for reparatory justice, telling a high-level conference in Ghana that historical injustices continue to shape inequalities across the continent and the global African diaspora. Speaking at the Next Step: High-Level Consultative Conference on Reparatory Justice for Africans and People of African Descent in Accra, Nandi-Ndaitwah said Africa’s campaign for reparations was not about reopening historical wounds but confronting legacies that continue to affect millions of Africans and people of African descent. The conference, hosted by Ghana under the leadership of President John Mahama, brought together heads of state, former leaders and policymakers to discuss implementation of a landmark UN resolution on slavery and reparatory justice and the future direction of Africa’s campaign for historical redress. The intervention by the Namibian leader was significant because it connected Namibia’s quest for justice over colonial-era atrocities to the wider continental effort seeking recognition of the enduring consequences of slavery, colonialism and racial exploitation. ‘Africa is not seeking to open old wounds. Africa is seeking to heal the wounds that were never healed,’ Nandi-Ndaitwah told delegates. The gathering forms part of Ghana’s broader effort to advance the African Union reparations agenda, with Mahama serving as the AU’s designated champion on reparations. Reparations campaign enters new phase Nandi-Ndaitwah said Africa had reached a critical moment in its pursuit of historical justice and called on governments to transform commitments into action. Her remarks come as support grows for a global campaign for slavery reparations backed by African, Caribbean and other Global South governments seeking to move the debate from recognition towards implementation. She argued that the recently adopted UN resolution represented a major step forward but should be viewed as the beginning rather than the end of the process. ‘It is the beginning of a journey towards truth, acknowledgement, healing and justice for millions of Africans and people of African descent whose lives were forever changed by slavery, colonialism and historical injustice,’ she said. The Namibian leader said the effects of slavery and colonial rule remain visible through inequality, poverty, lost opportunities and the continuing search by descendants of enslaved Africans for their identities, cultures and ancestral connections. Namibia draws lessons from genocide negotiations The president said Namibia’s own experience demonstrated both the complexity and importance of pursuing restorative justice. She recalled that Namibia’s parliament adopted a motion in 2006 calling for recognition of the genocide committed against the Herero and Nama communities between 1904 and 1908, alongside demands for an apology and reparations. According to Nandi-Ndaitwah, Namibia has spent the past nine years engaging Germany on the issue. She presented the negotiations as evidence that the pursuit of historical justice requires persistence and sustained political engagement. ‘The process of negotiation has not always been easy. It requires patience, resilience and unwavering commitment to dialogue,’ she said. ‘One lesson we have learned is that justice is not really a straightforward road. It is often slow and uncomfortable. However, we remain engaged as a solution has to be found.’ Germany formally recognised the killings as genocide in 2021. The atrocities claimed tens of thousands of Herero and Nama lives during German colonial rule in what is now Namibia, but discussions over compensation, reparations and reconciliation have remained politically sensitive. The discussions are taking place against the backdrop of an intensifying global reparations debate that has exposed divisions between African countries and several Western governments over historical accountability and redress. Nandi-Ndaitwah argued that lasting reconciliation could only be achieved through ‘truth, acknowledgment and mutual respect’. Genocide remembrance becomes national policy The president also highlighted recent measures taken by Namibia to confront its past. She said Namibia has designated May 28 as a national Genocide Remembrance Day and public holiday, describing the move as part of a broader effort to preserve historical memory and promote healing. Nandi-Ndaitwah noted that she launched the observance in 2025 and that commemorations were held nationwide for the first time this year. She also referred to efforts to repatriate the remains of Namibians removed during the colonial period and transported to Germany for scientific study and museum collections. ‘Their return is not merely a matter of history. It is a matter of humanity, dignity and closure for generations that continue to carry this burden,’ she said. Call for unity and diaspora engagement Nandi-Ndaitwah urged African countries to remain united in pursuing reparatory justice and warned against divisions that had historically weakened African causes. She also called for greater participation by the African diaspora in continental affairs, noting that the African Union formally recognises the diaspora as Africa’s ‘sixth region’. ‘We may come from different countries and speak different languages, but our collective future depends on our ability to stand together around a common purpose,’ she said. The president said reparatory justice was not solely about financial compensation but also about restoring dignity, confidence, identity and historical truth. Ghana praised for leadership Nandi-Ndaitwah commended President Mahama and Ghana for convening the conference and helping advance the continent’s reparatory justice agenda. She described Ghana as a natural venue for the discussions because of its historic connection to the transatlantic slave trade and its longstanding role in African liberation movements and Pan-African cooperation. Concluding her address, the Namibian leader urged African governments, institutions and diaspora communities to remain united in pursuing justice and reconciliation. ‘History has brought us to this moment. The question before us is whether we have the courage, readiness and unity to finish the work that previous generations began,’ she said.The post Namibia links Germany genocide talks to reparations push first appeared on Africa Briefing.

Keypoints: Pratt calls Macron’s participation in reparations conference ‘unacceptable’ • Ghanaian activist seeks legal claims against institutions linked to slavery • Speech outlines roadmap for global reparations campaign GHANAIAN journalist and activist Kwesi Pratt Jnr has described French President Emmanuel Macron’s participation in a high-level conference on reparations for the transatlantic slave trade as ‘totally unacceptable’, arguing that former colonial powers should face demands for repair rather than offer symbolic expressions of sympathy. Pratt made the remarks on June 19 at the Next Step: High-Level Consultative Conference on the Landmark United Nations Resolution on the Trafficking of Enslaved Africans, where he also called for a coordinated global reparations campaign. His proposals included legal claims against governments, banks, corporations and other institutions that benefited from the transatlantic slave trade, as well as the creation of a permanent Africa-diaspora reparations mechanism. The two-day conference in Accra focused on how to translate a recent UN General Assembly resolution on the trafficking of enslaved Africans and racialised chattel enslavement into practical action. The resolution builds on efforts including Ghana’s campaign for a UN resolution on slavery reparations, which helped elevate the issue on the international agenda. Advocates view the resolution as an important diplomatic milestone in efforts to advance reparatory justice and historical accountability. The resolution is widely viewed by campaigners as one of the most significant international acknowledgements to date of the historical impact of the transatlantic slave trade on Africa and its diaspora. Macron criticism sparks controversy Pratt reserved some of his strongest language for Macron’s involvement in the conference. Speaking before delegates from Africa and the diaspora, he argued that discussions about reparations should not become platforms for symbolic expressions of sympathy from countries connected to slavery and colonialism. ‘This should not be a forum for hollow expressions of sympathy and the propaganda of perpetrators of the crimes for which we demand and seek repair,’ he said. Pratt further described Macron’s participation as ‘totally unacceptable’, remarks that are likely to generate debate among supporters and critics of the international reparations movement. Pratt’s criticism reflects broader frustration among some African and diaspora reparations advocates. In a recent social media post ahead of the conference, Swiss-Cameroonian activist Nathalie Yamb compared Macron’s participation to ‘inviting a rapist to his victim’s therapy session’. The remark reflected the intensity of feeling among some campaigners who argue that former colonial powers have yet to meaningfully address demands for reparatory justice. France has increasingly sought to reset relations with African countries following military withdrawals from several former colonies in West Africa and growing criticism of its historical role on the continent. The debate intensified following Ghana’s challenge to France after the UN slavery vote, which renewed scrutiny of how former colonial powers should engage with reparations discussions. At the same time, France, Britain, Portugal, Spain, Belgium and the Netherlands have all faced renewed scrutiny over their historical roles in the transatlantic slave trade and colonial expansion. From recognition to repair While the Macron criticism attracted attention, the central message of Pratt’s speech focused on moving beyond symbolic recognition. He described the UN resolution as a historic breakthrough in the struggle to secure international recognition of the transatlantic slave trade as a crime against humanity. However, he argued that recognition alone would not address the enduring consequences of slavery, colonialism and economic extraction. ‘From recognition, we must move to repair,’ Pratt told delegates, framing reparations as a matter of justice rather than charity. According to him, millions of Africans were forcibly removed from their communities over several centuries, contributing to long-term demographic, political and economic disruptions that continue to influence the continent’s development. Pratt acknowledged that some African actors participated in aspects of the slave trade, but argued that historical complexity should not obscure responsibility. He maintained that European imperial and commercial powers were the principal architects, organisers and beneficiaries of the system. Building a reparations framework A key proposal in Pratt’s address was the creation of a permanent reparations mechanism bringing together the African Union, CARICOM, African governments, diaspora organisations, economists, historians, legal experts and cultural institutions. He said the body should coordinate research, advocacy, negotiations and implementation efforts while helping to establish a unified African and diaspora position on reparatory justice. Pratt also called for legal investigations into governments, monarchies, banks, corporations, universities, churches and insurance firms that profited from slavery. He argued that historical records should be opened, profits traced and responsibility established through legal and diplomatic channels. Development and cultural restoration Pratt stressed that reparations should not be limited to financial compensation. Among the measures he proposed were debt cancellation, development financing, industrial support, technology transfer, educational investment and healthcare strengthening. He also called for the return of African artefacts held in foreign museums, arguing that cultural restitution should be treated as a legal and moral obligation rather than an act of generosity. According to Pratt, the transatlantic slave trade was not only an economic crime but also an assault on African identities, languages, cultures and collective memory. As a result, he said reparatory justice must include memorial projects, museums, archives, return journeys, cultural exchanges and efforts to restore African dignity and historical memory. Growing momentum for reparatory justice The speech reflects growing momentum behind reparations campaigns across Africa and the Caribbean. The growing momentum has also been reflected at the continental level. The African Union designated 2025 as the Year of Reparations, signalling increased political support for efforts to secure historical justice, restitution and reparatory measures for Africa and its diaspora. Recent initiatives, including South Africa’s support for a continent-wide reparations agenda, have reinforced calls for coordinated African action on historical justice and restitution. Governments and advocacy groups have increasingly coordinated their efforts through the African Union and CARICOM, arguing that present-day global inequalities cannot be fully understood without acknowledging the legacy of slavery and colonialism. Former colonial powers have generally resisted formal reparations programmes, arguing that contemporary governments cannot be held directly liable for actions committed centuries ago. Reparations advocates counter that many institutions continue to benefit from wealth and influence accumulated during those periods. For Pratt, the recent UN resolution creates a new opportunity to move the debate beyond recognition. The challenge for advocates now is whether Africa can convert moral arguments into concrete outcomes, a question explored in Africa Briefing’s analysis of whether reparations demands can be translated into tangible results. ‘The real question is whether we have the courage to repair what was broken,’ he told delegates.  The post Macron presence at reparations forum ‘unacceptable’ first appeared on Africa Briefing.
